bio.en: Jason Feifer is editor-in-chief of Entrepreneur Magazine, a startup advisor, author, and podcast host who gets deeply tactical about how founders can earn press.
bio.zh: Jason Feifer 是《Entrepreneur》杂志的主编、创业顾问、作家兼播客主持人，他非常具体地讲解创始人如何获得媒体曝光。

summary.en: Jason reframes the journalist's mindset: editors and writers don't care about you, they care about their audience—so pitch how you can help them serve readers, not as a service provider. He covers how to find and pitch the right journalist (freelancers are often more responsive), why a publication's mission must shape your pitch, which channels to use to reach out, and how to define what success from press actually looks like. It's a pragmatic, no-nonsense guide to getting coverage for your product.
summary.zh: Jason 重新框定了记者的心态：编辑和记者不在乎你，他们在乎的是读者——所以你的 pitch 要说明你能如何帮他们服务读者，而不是把他们当服务商。他讲了如何找到并对正确的记者出手（自由撰稿人往往更积极）、为何媒体的使命必须塑造你的 pitch、用哪些渠道去联系，以及如何定义“拿到曝光”真正的成功标准。这期节目是关于为产品争取报道的务实、去水分的指南。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: The editor, the writer, I'll just say it as plainly as possible. They don't care about you. They don't care about you. They care about their reader or their listener or their viewer. That's who they care about. That's who they're serving, and if you can be of use to them in sharing the kinds of information that they are looking to serve their audience, then you can get what you want. But you can't treat them like a service provider because they're not. And so you have to approach them with an understanding of what they're trying to do for their audience and how you can fit into that because if you don't, they are not interested in you.
turns.zh: 编辑、作者，我要把话说得再明白不过。他们不在乎你。他们不在乎你。他们在乎的是他们的读者、听众或观众。这才是他们关心的对象。这才是他们服务的对象。如果你能为他们提供他们想为受众服务的那类信息，那你就能得到你想要的。但你不能把他们当作服务提供商，因为他们不是。所以你必须带着对他们试图为受众做什么的理解去接近他们，以及你如何能融入其中——因为如果你做不到，他们对你就没兴趣。

But one of the great insights that you can get into the challenges of that industry is how completely automated a lot of it is where a lot of people in PR are not thinking specifically about how to tell the right story to the right potential media outlet. I have... Entrepreneur Magazine is the thing that people obviously would pitch, but then I have this newsletter where I don't interview anybody. There's no opportunity to be featured in my newsletter, and I still get pitches to the newsletter because somebody saw it and dropped it in some spreadsheet, and it just... now I get it. turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 好的。接下来我们要深入探讨如何才能做好这件事，但先再问几个问题来搭建背景。第一个是关于影响力的问题。创业公司获得媒体报道后，对产品增长有何实际影响？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: So it's a really wide range. I have had entrepreneurs tell me that a single story in Entrepreneur Magazine, like the print magazine or just online, will drive more, whatever more app downloads, more sales that month than any of their paid marketing efforts. (00:08:16): But then I have also heard entrepreneurs tell me that it didn't do anything for them or that it did one very specific thing for them, which is to say maybe some potential partner read it and reached out, and it started an interesting conversation. It's all over the gamut, and it's a really important thing for people to remember is that this is not something that I think that you should bank on as a strategy for growth. It's a great add-on. But if you think that press by itself is going to solve your problems, you're wrong because it might, but it's way too unpredictable.
turns.zh: 影响范围很广。我曾听创业者说，在《创业者》杂志（无论是纸质版还是网络版）上发表一篇文章，能比他们任何付费营销活动带来更多下载量、更多当月销售额。（00:08:16）但我也听过创业者说，这对他们毫无用处，或者只带来了一项具体成果，比如某个潜在合作伙伴读了文章后主动联系，开启了有益的合作。影响程度不一。重要的是要记住，这不应被视为增长策略的核心。它是锦上添花的手段。但如果你指望媒体报道能单独解决问题，那就错了。它或许能起作用，但成功概率太低了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there anything else along those lines of just when it's worth somebody investing time into getting press, either stage of startup, type of startup, any just general broad advice of you should not be spending time on trying to get press versus this is a really good opportunity for you.
turns.zh: 还有其他类似的问题吗？比如在创业的哪个阶段、何种类型的创业公司值得投入时间获取媒体报道？有没有通用建议，比如何时不该花时间争取媒体曝光，何时又是个绝佳机会？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Think about press the same way that you think about raising money, which is to say you do it when you know what the money is for, and you should do it when you know what the press is for. A lot of people reach out to me at such an early stage that if we wrote about them, it wouldn't get them anything. They're not at a stage where they could use that press in any meaningful way, and so there's really no purpose in chasing it now. You should step back and think really as a starting point, "What do I need press for?" And if you have a good tactical answer to that, that could be because I need to drive awareness to a new product. That could be because I'm going out to raise money, and I need articles to show that the marketplace takes me seriously. (00:09:55): These are good reasons, but I get a lot of emails. It's funny because people are... like entrepreneurs, in particular, they're just so vulnerable, and it's kind of a wonderful way sometimes. And sometimes people will just email me, and they'll just say, "You know, I've worked really hard, and I just feel like I deserve this." I respect that, and I relate to it in some ways with my own trying to get attention for my own work. But, "I deserve this" that's not a good tactical decision for your business that doesn't do anything for you. And so I would put that to the side and only think of press as you don't go out and raise money if you don't know what the money is for. You shouldn't go out and try to get press if you don't know what the press is for.
turns.zh: 想想获取媒体报道这件事，就跟筹集资金一样。也就是说，当你清楚资金用途时才去筹集，同样，当你清楚媒体报道的意义所在时才应该去争取。很多人在我事业初期就找我合作，但如果我们为他们写文章，根本起不到任何实际效果——因为他们尚未达到能有效利用媒体资源的阶段。所以现在去追逐媒体关注实在没有意义。你应该先退一步，认真思考：“我为什么需要媒体报道？”如果能给出合理的策略性答案，比如“我要为新产品提升知名度”，或者“我正筹集资金，需要用文章证明市场对我的认可”，这些都是不错的理由。（00:09:55）但我收到太多邮件了。有趣的是，人们……尤其是创业者，他们太容易受伤，有时这种脆弱感还挺令人心疼。有些人会发邮件说：“我真的很努力，我觉得自己值得拥有这些。”我尊重这种情怀，甚至能在一定程度上共鸣，因为我自己也曾为作品寻求关注。但“我值得拥有”这种想法对商业来说并非明智之选，既不能帮你达成目标。我建议把这种想法抛开。就像筹集资金前要先明确用途一样，获取媒体报道也应基于清晰的策略性考量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm curious to hear other examples when it's not, when it's a bad idea because, as like I said, an outside observer, I would always love to get more attention for my product and more people to be aware of it, more people to check it out. turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Oftentimes, it's not even about the moment, but it's about the publication. So I'll give you an example. I spoke at an event once, and afterwards, this guy comes up to me, and he has a small hot dog food truck business in Washington, DC. So he said he's got a couple trucks, and he's doing good business selling hot dogs, and he wants coverage in Entrepreneur Magazine. He's like, "Oh, how can I get a feature?" And the problem with that instinct that he has is that he's really directing his energy in the wrong place because if he is selling hot dogs in Washington, DC, then I understand what press is for him. Press is to drive hotdog sales. That's what he wants to do. Entrepreneur is not going to do that for him. Full stop. Why? Because Entrepreneur reaches a national to international audience. (00:11:52): So that means that 99.5% of the people who would read a story about this guy have no ability to go get his hotdogs, which means that that was wasted effort. So fine. Was it that hard to come up and talk to me at the conference? No. But scale that out. How many emails is he sending that are like that? How much energy is he putting into chasing things that ultimately don't have good direct value to him? What he needs to do is think, "Okay, my goal, get more people to buy hot dogs. Where am I? I'm in Washington, DC. How can I reach people who are interested in food in my market?" So stop chasing Entrepreneur and start chasing the local eater or the food section of the Washingtonian or something like that. That small shift can give you a lot more payoff for your effort.
turns.zh: 很多时候，关键不在于当下，而是在于发布平台。让我举个例子。我曾在一场活动上发言，之后有个家伙过来找我。他在华盛顿特区经营着一家小型热狗餐车生意。他说自己有几辆餐车，在卖热狗方面做得很不错，还想在《企业家》杂志上获得报道。他问：“哦，那要怎么才能获得专题报道呢？” 但他的这种想法其实方向错了。因为他在华盛顿特区卖热狗，那么媒体报道对他来说应该有助于促进销售，这才是他真正需要的。但《企业家》杂志的读者群体面向全国乃至全球，99.5%的读者都无法到他那里买热狗，这根本是徒劳之举。那么，直接来找我交流又有多难呢？不难。但放大来看，他发送了多少类似的邮件？又投入了多少精力去追逐对自己毫无直接价值的东西？他需要想清楚：“好吧，我的目标是让更多人买热狗。我在哪里？我在华盛顿特区。怎样才能接触到本地对美食感兴趣的人？” 所以别再追逐《企业家》杂志了，去追逐当地媒体，比如《华盛顿人》美食版块之类的。这种小小的转变能让你的努力事半功倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a good segue to just let's just dive into how to actually go about getting press, and I know you-
turns.zh: 接下来就来具体探讨如何获取媒体报道吧，我知道你们——

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... kind of have this three-step structure for thinking about it. Maybe just start with what are the three steps, and then we'll dive into each one.
turns.zh: ……我有个三步法的思路，或许可以先从三个步骤讲起。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, sure. So I mean, look, it is pretty simple, right. Step one is prep. You want to be thinking about how to tell your story. You want to be thinking about the kinds of stuff I just talked about. What is press for for you? Everything that you need to do to orient yourself towards what is this opportunity, and why am I chasing it, and how to make the most of it. Step two is figuring out who to pitch. Not all press is created equal. There are not reasons to just go chasing everybody arbitrarily. The hotdog example is a good one. (00:13:19): So finding the writers and editors who you're actually going to reach out to, who are going to most receptive to you. And also making sure that because you did the prep, you can figure out how to tell your story in a way that they're going to be interested in. We'll talk about that. And then step three is the actual pitch. What does it mean to reach out to these people, to engage the writers and editors? How do you find them? What do you send them? What are you telling them? That's it. (00:13:42): I mean, right. But what you need to understand is that you're entering a world that probably doesn't operate the way in which you think it does, and I see that all the time as the recipient of pitches. People don't understand who they're reaching out to and how I and my colleagues think. We should maybe even start with that because a really important thing to understand just again, to go to [inaudible 00:14:07]-
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。我是说，步骤很简单，对吧。第一步是准备。你要思考如何讲述自己的故事。要考虑我刚才提到的那些问题：媒体对你的意义是什么？你需要做哪些准备工作来明确机会所在、追逐目标的意义，以及如何充分利用机会。第二步是确定目标受众。不是所有媒体都一样的，没必要盲目联系所有人。热狗餐车案例就是个很好的例子。（00:13:19）所以要找到最有可能接受你的记者和编辑，同时确保你已经做好准备，能用他们感兴趣的方式讲述你的故事。接下来我们会详细探讨。第三步是实际的提案。如何联系这些人，如何吸引编辑和记者？如何找到他们？发送什么内容？说什么话？就是这些。（00:13:42）嗯，没错。但你要明白，你即将进入一个可能与你想象截然不同的领域，作为被联系方，我经常遇到这种情况。人们不了解对方是谁，也不了解我和同事的想法。我们或许应该先从这点讲起，因为理解这些非常重要，这样才能——（00:14:07，语音中断）

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:14:07] do it. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: ... yeah, the metaphor of the investors, you don't reach out to an investor if you don't understand what that investor does, what they're interested in, or what kinds of companies they invest in. You can't do that with media, either. So I get pitches every single day along the lines of, "How do I get coverage in Entrepreneur Magazine? How do I get a feature in Entrepreneur Magazine?" And to me, it always feels like they're ordering a hamburger from me. Like, "How do I get a hamburger from Entrepreneur Hamburgers, right?" They're treating me like a service provider. That my job is to provide press. (00:14:44): And I get it because, of course, if you're an entrepreneur, and you're looking for press, then the... [inaudible 00:14:51] writers and editors out there seem to be in the business of writing about people, and therefore, there's some service that they seem to provide, and you're trying to figure out how to get it. But that's not how the media thinks of themselves, right. The editor, the writer, I'll just say it as plainly as possible, they don't care about you. They don't care about you. They care about their reader, or their listener, or their viewer. (00:15:18): That's who they care about. That's who they're serving. And if you can be of use to them in sharing the kinds of information that they are looking to serve their audience, then you can get what you want, but you can't treat them like a service provider because they're not. And so you have to approach them with an understanding of what they're trying to do for their audience and how you can fit into that. Because if you don't, they are not interested in you.
turns.zh: ……是啊，用投资者作比喻，如果你不了解投资者的业务、他们的兴趣所在，以及他们投资的公司类型，你就没法去找他们合作。媒体行业也是如此。我每天都会收到诸如“如何在《创业者》杂志获得报道？如何在《创业者》杂志获得专题报道？”之类的提问。对我而言，这感觉就像他们在向我点餐似的。比如，“我要怎么从《创业者汉堡店》买到汉堡呢？”他们把我当成了服务提供商，觉得我的工作就是提供新闻曝光。（00:14:44）我能理解这种心态，毕竟如果你是一位创业者，在寻求媒体报道时，那些记者和编辑似乎专注于报道人物故事，因此你总想找到获取报道的捷径。但媒体从业者自己可不这么想，对吧。编辑和记者说得再直白一点，他们不在乎你。他们不在乎你，他们在乎他们的读者、听众或观众。（00:15:18）这才是他们关心的群体，也是他们服务的对象。如果你能提供有价值的信息，帮助他们满足读者需求，那你就能得到想要的结果。但你不能把他们当成服务提供商，因为他们不是。所以你必须带着这样的理解去接近他们：他们想为读者创造什么样的价值？你如何能融入他们的服务体系？因为若不然，他们根本没兴趣理会你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And more... even specifically, what is it they're trying to do for their audience? I imagine it's just have something interesting that they want to read. Something they can learn. Something they're like, "Wow, I'm really excited to read this."
turns.zh: 我太赞同了。更具体地说，他们想为读者提供什么样的价值？我想应该是让读者读到有趣的内容，学到新知识，产生那种“哇，真期待读到这篇文章”的惊喜感。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah. But it's going to be more specific based on the mission of each publication. So, for example, I've worked at two separate business titles. I was a senior editor at Fast Company for a number of years, and now I'm the editor-in-chief of Entrepreneur Magazine. The decision that is made about whether or not a story belongs in a publication, it was totally different based on these two publications. So I can't speak to Fast Company now because they've gone through a couple of leadership changes. I don't know what their mission is, but back when I worked there under Bob Safian, he was the editor-in-chief, that was really a magazine about where businesses going, and the stories that were in the magazine were all supposed to be in some way representative of the evolution of business. (00:16:50): And so when people would pitch what we'd really be looking for are, are there insights into... in what this person is doing that other people could read and say, "Aha, that helps me understand where this industry is going or that industry, or it helps me think about how I can shape my own company to match current trends," that kind of stuff. Entrepreneur, totally different mission. The way that I think of Entrepreneur is that it's not even a magazine about business. It's a magazine about thinking. Or what I want to do is make sure that everybody who comes to the magazine walks away with great insights into how to think through the challenges in their business. (00:17:29): And so what I'm looking for when somebody reaches out is did they make some interesting counterintuitive decision that solved a problem in their business, and I'll emphasize in. Because, oftentimes, when people hear me talk about solving problems in business, they think, "Aha, but I solve a problem in business, right. I saw that there weren't the best razors in the world, and I made the best razors." That's not what I'm talking about. What I'm talking about is... There's this woman whose name is Joelle Mertzel. She has a company called Kitchen Concepts Unlimited, and she makes a butter dish, and it's a really smart butter dish because it is built on a hinge, right. So this is designed to solve a very specific problem, which Lenny, I don't know if you knew this, I did not, that you don't need to refrigerate butter. Did you know that?
turns.zh: 是的。但这会根据每个出版物的使命而有所不同。比如，我曾在两家不同的商业类刊物工作过。我在《快公司》担任了数年的高级编辑，现在则担任《创业家》杂志的主编。判断一篇报道是否适合某本刊物，依据这两家出版物是截然不同的。现在我无法谈论《快公司》了，因为他们经历了多次领导层变动。不知道他们现在的使命是什么，但我记得在Bob Safian担任主编时，我在那里工作，那本杂志主要关注商业发展趋势，刊登的文章都应在某种程度上体现商业进化轨迹。（00:16:50）所以当人们提案时，我们真正寻找的是——有没有对某个行业发展的深刻洞察，能让读者读后感叹“原来行业是这样发展的，或者这能启发我如何顺应潮流调整自己的公司”之类的内容。《创业家》的使命则完全不同。在我看来，《创业家》甚至不只是一本商业杂志，更是一本关于思考的杂志。我的核心理念是，要确保每位读者都能从中获得深刻的思维启发，学会如何应对商业挑战。（00:17:29）所以当有人向我推荐选题时，我会特别关注他们是否做出过非传统的决策来解决商业难题。我强调这一点是因为，人们一听到“解决商业难题”往往会联想到“我发现市面上没有优质剃须刀，于是自己研发出最好的剃须刀”之类的故事。但我指的并非此类。举个例子，Joelle Mertzel创立的Kitchen Concepts Unlimited公司，开发了一款巧妙的黄油碟，采用铰链设计，专门解决一个现实难题——无需冷藏黄油。莱尼，你可能不知道这个知识点，我之前也不知道。其实我们完全可以不冷藏黄油，你知道吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I knew that intellectually, but I still refrigerate it. I know people don't.
turns.zh: 我虽然理性上知道这一点，但现实中还是习惯冷藏黄油。不过我知道很多人不这么做。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Me too, even though I've had multiple conversations with this woman about this. You don't need to refrigerate butter, and if you leave it out, it cuts easier. It's more spreadable. Big problem, the butter dish. So most butter dishes you just lift up. And so if you have warm room temperature butter that's soft, and you lift the butter dish top up, you might bump into the butter, and it's going to make a big mess. So Joelle makes a butter dish on a hinge, right. Opens and closes exactly the same way every single time. No mess. Brilliant, solves a problem. She reaches out to me about this. This is not interesting to us, right. Maybe this is interesting for a cooking magazine, right. Maybe Bon Appétit is interested in this. Entrepreneur's not interested in this because that doesn't help other entrepreneurs to have thought through that problem. (00:19:13): But then she tells me something else. What she tells me is that she is, at the very beginning of this, trying to figure out how to answer some basic questions about her audience, like what colors do they want in this butter dish and what price point are they willing to pay? And she wants to do some market research. She goes to a market research company. She says, "How much would it cost to research consumers and answer these questions?" They say, $10,000. She doesn't have $10,000. And then, one day, she's sitting at the airport waiting to board a flight, and she looks around and she realizes that airports are full of people who have absolutely nothing better to do than answer questions about butter dishes, right. Nothing better to do, just sitting there. And you could start at gate one. By the time you get to gate eight, everyone in gate one is new. You could do it all over again, and you could have a 6:00 PM flight, and you could show up at 9:00 AM. Nobody's going to stop you. You can do this all day in the airport. And this is how she starts to do her own market research. She saves that $10,000, and she does it herself. I put that story in the magazine. It's tiny. It's this tiny random company and this random decision. But the reason I did it is because every time I repeat that story to entrepreneurs, they're all like, "Ugh, right, totally. There's always other ways to do things." They love the ingenuity of it. That's what I'm looking for. That's Entrepreneur's stories. So to go back to the point that you were making, it's not just about, "Well, it's a magazine called Entrepreneur. They must write about entrepreneurs, right. I'm an entrepreneur. I belong in Entrepreneur." (00:20:41): People think that all the time. No. You have to step back and read what these publications are publishing and ask yourself, "What are they doing? What is the purpose here?" The editors and the writers, they're making decisions about what goes in this magazine, and they're making decisions about how the stories are constructed. Why are they doing that? Who are they trying to reach? When you start to see it through that lens, you start to see the pattern, and you get an understanding a real instruction manual for what it actually means to pitch these publications.
turns.zh: 我也这么觉得，尽管我已经和这位女士就此事讨论过多次了。你不需要把黄油放进冰箱，如果放在室温下，切起来更容易，也更容易涂抹。但黄油盒是个大问题。大多数黄油盒都是直接提起的。当你提起黄油盒顶部时，黄油可能会洒出来，弄得一团糟。所以乔艾尔设计了一个带铰链的黄油盒，打开和关闭的方式每次都完全一样，不会有任何混乱。真是天才之作，完美解决了这个问题。她向我提起这个想法。但我们当时觉得这没什么意思，对吧？或许这对烹饪杂志有吸引力，对吧？《Bon Appétit》可能会感兴趣。但《Entrepreneur》对此不感兴趣，因为这对其他创业者没有帮助去思考这个问题。（00:19:13）但后来她告诉我另一件事。她最初想弄清楚如何回答一些关于目标受众的基本问题，比如他们希望黄油盒是什么颜色，愿意支付什么价格？于是她去找了一家市场调研公司，问：“研究消费者并回答这些问题需要多少钱？”对方报价1万美元。她没那么多钱。后来有一天，她在机场候机时，环顾四周，意识到机场到处都是无所事事的人，他们最喜欢做的事就是回答关于黄油盒的问题，对吧？没别的事可做，就坐在那里。你从一号登机口开始，等你走到八号登机口时，第一个登机口的人又都是新面孔。你可以从头再来一次，甚至可能搭下午6点的航班，早上9点就到机场。没人会阻止你。你可以在机场一整天都做这个。这就是她如何开始自己进行市场调研的。她省下了1万美元，自己动手做了这件事。我把这个故事写进了杂志。篇幅很小。这是一家小小的随机公司，做出一个随机决定。但我这么做的原因是，每次我把这个故事讲给创业者听，他们都会感叹：“啊，对啊，完全正确。总有其他解决问题的方法。”他们喜欢这种巧思。这正是我所追寻的。这才是《Entrepreneur》的故事。所以回到你之前提到的观点，不只是因为这是一本叫《Entrepreneur》的杂志，他们就必须写关于创业者的内容，对吧？我也是创业者，我属于《Entrepreneur》。但人们总是这么想。不对。你得退一步，仔细阅读这些出版物的内容，问自己：“他们的目的是什么？他们想传达什么信息？” 编辑和作者们决定杂志的内容，决定如何构思故事。他们为什么要这样做？他们想接触哪些读者？当你从这个角度去看，你就能发现其中的规律，也就能理解如何向这些出版物投稿的真正诀窍了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such an interesting insight. I had no idea that that was something you should be thinking about. Is there an easy way to understand the mission of the publication? Is there an about page they often add this to or is it, like you said, you just read a bunch of stuff and try to suss it out?
turns.zh: 这真是很有趣的见解。我之前完全没想到这也是需要考虑的。有没有简单的方法能理解出版物的使命？他们通常会在“关于我们”页面添加相关信息，还是像你说的，就是多读点东西，自己去领悟？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Nobody publishes an about page in that way because the internal logic of the editorial team. But you can certainly make some starting assumptions based on who the publication is trying to reach. Everybody is trying to reach somebody. It gets more complicated the more general interest something becomes, right. What is the New York Times? (00:21:53): What is the mission? That's a hard thing to answer. You sort of have to divide it up into sections, right. The mission of the National News Desk is different from the mission of the Business Desk, and even within there, the mission of the Sunday business section is different from the mission of the Monday to Saturday business section.
turns.zh: 没有人会以那种方式发布“关于我们”页面，这是因为编辑团队的内部逻辑所致。不过，你当然可以根据该媒体试图吸引的读者群体做出一些初步假设。毕竟，每个人都在试图触达特定人群。随着内容受众面越广，事情就越复杂，对吧？《纽约时报》又是什么样的呢？（00:21:53）：它的使命是什么？这个问题很难回答。你得把它拆分成几个部分，对吧。国家新闻部的使命和商业新闻部的使命不同，即便在商业新闻部内部，周日商业版块的使命也与周一至周六商业版块的使命有所差异。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: [inaudible 00:22:09].

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: So you have to start to really parse it out. And this is the reason why people hire PR is because if they're good at their jobs, they understand a lot of this already. But I really do think that if you spent time with the content and your starting point is, "I understand that this publication is trying to reach X. They're trying to reach these people," then you can start to see the patterns of what it is that they're doing. How are they telling stories? What do these five stories all have in common? They have something in common. There's something that they're all doing, and you can certainly read the tea leaves and try to figure it out.
turns.zh: 所以你必须真正去剖析其中的逻辑。这就是人们聘请公关公司的原因——因为如果他们工作出色的话，他们早已对此了如指掌。但我确实认为，如果你深入研究内容，并以"我知道这家媒体试图触达X群体，他们正努力吸引这些读者"为出发点，那么你就能逐渐发现他们的运作模式。他们是如何讲故事的？这五个新闻故事有何共同之处？它们确实存在共通之处，总有一些共同的做法，你完全可以解读其中的微妙之处并试图破解其中的奥秘。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay. It feels like we've already gone into step one around prep. What else is involved in preparing to get press?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，感觉我们已经进入了准备阶段的第一个步骤。准备获得媒体报道还涉及哪些其他方面呢？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: If we're talking about prep, the very first thing that you need to do is what I had said earlier, which is just ask yourself, what do I need press for? And you need a good answer to that question. And once you have that, the next thing you should do is you should start to think about, "Well, what's interesting about my business? And oftentimes, it's not necessarily what you think, and you can be guided in a way by what's happening in step two, where you start to think about who you're trying to reach out to. Because, for example, the story that somebody might tell me at Entrepreneur is going to be different than the story that somebody might tell Cosmo. (00:23:42): There's a reason for a company to end up in, both Entrepreneur and Cosmo, right. Maybe the product is for young women. And so, Cosmo might be interested in some kind of product feature or including the product in a roundup of some kind of products. Whereas Entrepreneur would do the entrepreneur-focused story. What did this founder do? How they do they write? You can take your... You could think about your story and kind of break it up into a whole bunch of different little pieces and then figure out which piece goes to what media. But oftentimes, people make the mistake of trying to do that in reverse, which is to say that they kind of decide what narrative they would like to have out in the world, and then they just go around to different publications trying to sell them on that. I get that all the time. (00:24:34): A lot of my pitches that I'll receive in my inbox are somebody who hasn't really thought at all about what Entrepreneur publishes but instead just has something that they would like to get out into the world. I mean, a good kind of dumb example is, yesterday, somebody sent me an email about a company that had just hired a new president. I don't care about that. That's not useful to my audience at all. I'm sure that there is a trade publication, right. Let's say that there was a company in the restaurant industry. I'm sure that a trade publication that follows the blow by blow by blow of a restaurant industry might be interested in your new president. But I'm not because you hiring that new president isn't useful to my audience. Stories in Entrepreneur are not really about the person that I'm writing about. (00:25:23): They're really about the audience. They're really me serving the audience through the stories of the people I'm writing about. That's not useful. I wish that they had spent a moment and thought about that, but they didn't. So once you start to think about who it is that you're trying to reach, you can step back and say, "Well, what part of my journey is going to be most relevant to them? And I would push you to be really, really creative about it. Because if you go back to the Butterie example, the butter dish, that little funny story about the airport, I mean, who else is writing about that? It's not central to her story as a brand. It's not central to her sales pitch. It was-
turns.zh:
若谈及媒体宣传，首先你需要做的是我之前提到的——先问自己：我需要向媒体传递什么信息？对这个问题的回答至关重要。一旦确定了核心诉求，接下来你要思考：我的业务有何亮点？很多时候，答案并非你想象的那样。这里可以参考第二步的思路——明确目标受众。例如，若某产品面向年轻女性群体，《企业家》杂志和《Cosmo》杂志的报道重点必然不同。前者可能聚焦创业者的故事，后者则更关注产品特性或产品集锦推荐。

许多人常犯的错误是倒推思路：先设定理想的宣传框架，再四处推销。这类稿件常被我拒之门外。比如昨日收到的邮件，某公司新聘总裁的消息对我读者毫无价值。相反，若餐厅行业的贸易媒体想追踪某家新晋总裁的动态，那才符合他们的报道定位。

Entrepreneur的报道核心在于服务读者，通过人物故事传递价值。若你的内容只是简单罗列事实，缺乏叙事张力，就难以引起共鸣。Butterie公司的例子说明，产品背后的趣味故事可能吸引我们，但对品牌核心或销售策略毫无关联——这类内容在行业媒体中才有价值。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: ... central to her story as a brand, it's not central to her sales pitch. It was just for us. We were probably the only publication in the world who cared about that, but I really cared about it.
turns.zh: ...对她的品牌故事而言无关紧要，也不符合她的销售主张。只不过我们是全世界唯一对此感兴趣的媒体，而她恰好需要我们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, so just kind of summarizing what you shared, think about the goal. What are you trying to get out of press? Goals could be awareness of what we've done, something new, investor interest. What are some other common examples of goals that you see for trying to get press?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，总结一下你分享的内容。先想想你的目标是什么。你希望通过媒体报道获得什么？可能是提高品牌知名度、宣传新产品、吸引投资者的兴趣。还有哪些常见的媒体报道目标呢？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, awareness of something new. But also doesn't have to be awareness of something new, it could just be continued growth, trying to reach into a new marketplace. That's fine. Anything that's tied to growth or reaching a new customer base-
turns.zh: 是的，提升新产品的知名度。但不一定非得是新产品，可能是持续发展、开拓新市场——这都没问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: ... would make sense.
turns.zh: ……这样做很有道理。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes sense.
turns.zh: 这说得通。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: But it could also be that you're looking to position yourself in your own marketplace a little differently. I see, for example, a lot of people, a lot of big companies, keep knocking on my door because we don't just hear from startups, we hear from major companies as well who are pitching stories. I know why they want to be an entrepreneur. They want to be an entrepreneur because they're trying to position their brand as also being relevant to small business owners. It's helpful to have that kind of context because coverage an entrepreneur can help them go out to the marketplace and say, "Look, we're also reaching X, Y, Z people." (00:27:25): So sometimes it's not even about a conversion, but rather it's about a positioning and that's a good reason to also maybe put forward your executives. Sometimes it's just about establishing your CEO or your founder as an authority in a particular area because you want them to be more trustworthy, you want them to be invited to more conferences. Because all of that stuff draws more attention to the company, all sorts of reasons to do this stuff. And then trying to get in front of investors, trying to get in front of partners. Look, there's a million reasons why being visible can be useful, but you need to make sure you understand what you're actually trying to do.
turns.zh: 但也可能是你想在自己的市场中树立独特的形象。比如，我发现很多大公司都在找我们合作，因为不只是初创公司，许多大公司也会来 pitch 故事。我知道他们为什么想当企业家——因为他们想把品牌定位成与小企业主相关的。这种背景信息很有帮助，因为媒体报道能帮助企业向市场传达："看，我们也服务 X、Y、Z 类客户。"（00:27:25）：有时候这甚至不关乎转化，而是关于品牌定位——这也是让高管出镜的好理由。有时只需确立 CEO 或创始人在某个领域的权威地位，让他们更受信任、更受邀参加会议。所有这些都能提升公司关注度，所以做这些事的理由有很多，但你得确保清楚自己的真实目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. That was really helpful. So think about what goal you have in mind for getting press, pick a publication and understand their mission and what their goals are. And then think about some interesting stories that you could pitch them. Not just like we have a new president, but something that you think they'd be excited to share that connects with their mission.
turns.zh: 好的，太棒了。这真的很有帮助。所以先想好你希望通过媒体报道达成什么目标，选择合适的媒体，了解他们的使命和目标。然后构思一些有趣的故事来 pitch 给他们。别只是说"我们有新总裁了"，而是要找到能与他们的使命产生共鸣、让他们兴奋分享的内容。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Kind of on this topic, I know we want to talk about who to contact and how to figure out who to actually talk to. A couple of questions that come to mind. This is all a lot of work. Founders are really busy.
turns.zh: 说到这，我知道我们想讨论如何联系媒体、如何筛选合适的媒体。几个问题冒出来了。这工作量太大了，创始人都很忙。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, it's a lot.
turns.zh: 是啊，很耗时。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So begs the question, PR agencies, do you have a perspective on would you recommend working with PR agency? Is there a time when it makes to and doesn't make sense to?
turns.zh: 所以问题来了，公关公司，你们对合作有何建议？什么时候合作有意义，什么时候没意义？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, I mean it's a ton of work. Everything that I'm describing is a ton of work. And let me be clear, people succeed in getting press without doing any of the things that I'm describing because dumb luck happens in the world. You could very well just bang out an email to some random editor and they might like it. That is entirely possible. You could disregard everything that I've just said. What I'm really helping you do is try to optimize your approach. But yeah, hiring PR can cut out a lot of this. Now you're not doing this research yourself, you're not thinking through these challenges yourself. You're working with people who understand exactly how to identify the most interesting parts of your story and then turn them into good pitches. So why wouldn't everyone do that? The couple reasons. Number one, cost PR can be expensive, so you just have to factor that in. Number two, PR is and can be, I'll say can be, a very frustrating journey because a lot of PR people are very bad at their jobs. They're very bad. (00:29:52): And this isn't just me bashing PR people. I have literally been hired to give keynotes at PR industry conferences. And I get on stage and I say most PR people are bad at their jobs and everybody nods. And they all know it. And of course, none of them think that they're one of the bad ones, but they all know it. PR is full of people who are bad at their jobs. Why are they bad at their jobs? They're bad at their jobs because they're lazy, because they're primarily relying upon email blasts, just sending things out, because they have a older idea of what it means to get the word out. For example, if you hire or talk to a PR agency and one of the things that they recommend doing that you should spend money on is a press release, like a traditional press release, run as fast as you can away from that. I don't know if you know this. Do you know this? The press release, there are some purposeful reasons to put out a press release, but the press release is really no longer the primary unit of press attraction.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说这可是个大工程。我所描述的每一项工作都需要投入大量精力。说白了，有些人能不费吹灰之力就获得媒体关注，因为世事难料。说不定你随手给某位编辑发封邮件，他们就喜欢上了你的内容。这完全有可能。你大可以无视我刚刚说的一切。我真正想帮你做的，是优化你的策略。不过雇佣公关公司确实能省去很多麻烦。你无需自己做调研，也无需独自应对这些挑战。专业团队会帮你挖掘故事中最吸引人的亮点，并将其转化为优质的宣传提案。那么为什么不都这么做呢？有几个原因。首先，公关费用不菲，这点得考虑在内。其次，公关之路可能令人沮丧，因为很多公关人员业务能力欠佳。他们实在不怎么样。（00:29:52）这可不是我故意贬低公关人员。我曾受邀在公关行业会议上做主题演讲。站在台上时，我说大多数公关人员业务能力不足，台下所有人都点头认同。他们心里都清楚这一点，当然没人觉得自己是其中之一，但大家都心知肚明。公关行业充斥着不称职的人。他们为什么不称职？因为他们懒惰，因为他们主要依赖群发邮件、随意投稿，因为他们对宣传推广的理念已经过时了。比如，如果你雇佣公关公司，他们建议你花钱做传统新闻稿，那赶紧跑吧。你知道吗？新闻稿确实有特定场景可以用，但它已不再是吸引媒体关注的主要手段。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I get that sense.
turns.zh: 是啊，我能体会这种感受。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah. But here's what's fascinating. So a PR agency I wouldn't recommend might do this. They'll tell you, "We're going to put together a press release about this new thing, so you have to pay a little extra money for the production of this press release and then also the distribution of this press release because what we're going to do is we're going to put it out on the wire," because there are a whole bunch of press release distribution wires. So they'll do that, you'll pay the money, it'll go out on the wire. And then they'll send you a report about all the places that this press release ended up on. It ended up on Yahoo Finance, it ended up on Market Watch. And it technically did. The press release is there, it was posted. And zero people are going to see it in the whole world because Yahoo Finance has a section where they just publish every damn press release that gets published by all these different distributors. Nobody saw that. (00:32:08): So don't confuse posting press releases even on very big websites with actual success. What you want in an actual PR person is someone who traffics in one thing, and that is relationships. The most important thing that a PR person can have is active relationships with people in media. Why? If a PR person is guaranteeing you press, that's another reason to run out the door as fast as possible because the PR people cannot control this. Writers and editors, they do what they want. It's a completely subjective industry and very frustrating. I completely understand. That was totally subjective. So the best that a PR person can do is shape your story, understand who to pitch, and then get that writer or editor to look at it, to pay attention to it. There are some PR people in this world who I think very highly of. I think they're incredibly smart, incredibly good at what they do, and they only pitch me when they have something that they think I will genuinely be interested in. Instead of a lot of PR people who just send me some random thing every week or every day. (00:33:21): I don't pay attention to those people. But, I don't know, just shout out, when John Beer from Jack Taylor PR sends me ... John, I met him in a PR capacity a decade ago and we've since become friends. When he emails me, I pay attention. I don't write about it all the time. I'm not going to write about something just because I like John, but I will pay attention. And paying attention honestly is half the battle because people in media are getting so much email. So you want someone who's going to understand you, understand your industry, understand and know the people who they should be reaching out to, and who really respect you as an entrepreneur and are going to give you the hard feedback. Because there are a lot of people who will go and hire PR and they'll say, "I want you to email this and this and this and this and this publication." (00:34:16): And if the PR person just does that, all they're doing is annoying their contacts if they don't really feel like this was meaningful. You should like when a PR person pushes back on you and says, "You know what? I don't think that your story is right for that publication. Here's why." That's someone you should hire.
turns.zh: 是啊。但这里有件很有意思的事。有些我不推荐的公关公司可能会这么做。他们会跟你说：“我们要为这个新项目写一份新闻稿，所以你得额外付点钱来制作这份新闻稿，再加上分发费用，因为我们会把它发布到通讯社。”因为有各种各样的新闻稿分发平台。他们会这么做，你付了钱后，新闻稿确实会被发布到这些平台上。比如雅虎财经、Market Watch之类的。但实际上根本没人会看到这些新闻稿。雅虎财经有个专栏，里面堆满了各个分发商发来的新闻稿。根本没人会去看这些内容。（00:32:08）所以别把新闻稿发布到大网站就等同于取得成功了。真正需要的是专注于一件事——人脉维护。公关人员最重要的能力就是与媒体人建立积极的合作关系。为什么？如果公关公司保证你能获得媒体报道，那你最好赶紧跑路，因为媒体编辑不受公关公司的控制。他们想怎么做就怎么做。这是个完全主观的行业，非常令人沮丧。我完全理解这种情况。这完全是主观判断。所以公关人员能做的最好的事情就是帮你打磨故事，精准定位目标媒体，然后让编辑注意到你的内容。有一些公关人员我非常欣赏。他们极其聪明，业务能力超群，而且只有在他们认为我会真正感兴趣的情况下才会向我推荐内容，而不是像很多公关公司那样每周或每天都给我发些无关紧要的材料。（00:33:21）我对那些人根本不理会。不过，我也不知道，就点名表扬一下Jack Taylor PR的约翰·比尔吧。我十年前在公关活动上认识了他，后来成了朋友。他给我发邮件时，我都会仔细看。他不会一直催我写稿。我不会因为喜欢他就写，但我会留意。认真对待对方的需求很重要，因为媒体人每天收到太多邮件了。所以你需要一个能理解你、懂你的行业、清楚该联系哪些媒体、真正尊重你作为创业者的公关人员，并且能给你诚实反馈的人。毕竟很多人花钱请公关公司后，只会说：“你去给这家媒体发这份材料、那份材料、还有这份和那份。”（00:34:16）如果公关人员只是机械地执行，而没有真正的价值判断，那只会惹恼他们的联系人。你应该喜欢那种反驳你的公关人员，说：“你知道吗？我觉得你的故事不适合那家媒体。原因如下。”这样的人才值得合作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there any other PR people you want to call out as ones that you think are awesome?
turns.zh: 还有其他你想推荐的优秀公关人员吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: The challenge here is that I'm going to regret not including a whole bunch of people who don't pop to mind immediately, but-
turns.zh: 问题在于，我肯定会后悔没有提到很多现在没法立刻想到的人，但——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We can include them in the show notes, whoever else.
turns.zh: 没问题，我们可以把这些信息加到节目笔记里，还有其他人也可以。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, sure. Okay, so let's see. Off the top of my head, so John of Jack Taylor, he does a lot of wellness stuff. So PR agencies tend to specialize, and so you want to make sure that you're going with people who really understand you and the media ecosystem that you are reaching out to. So I think John's really smart. Let's see. Hannah Lee at Hannah Lee Communications is great on hospitality stuff. So restaurants, hotels, booze, they're really smart. Jen Sesquila, sorry Jen, if I mispronounced your name. Max Borges Agency, really good on sort of consumer focused products. Greg Delman, he's based in San Francisco, he has a boutique shop called G3 Media and he does a lot of tech startups stuff, just really knows that world. Greg, I'll find writers through Greg because he just knows everybody. I just texted him recently and I was like, "I need somebody who can write about this very specific AI thing." He happened to be at TechCrunch Disrupt and he found some freelancer and connected us. That's great. So those are four. I will have more that'll give you for the show notes.
turns.zh: 好的，没问题。让我想想。首先，《杰克·泰勒》的约翰，他做了很多健康相关的内容。公关公司通常都有专业分工，所以你得确保合作的团队真正了解你和你的目标媒体生态。约翰确实很专业。再看看。汉娜·李的Hannah Lee Communications在酒店业方面很拿手，比如餐厅、酒店、酒类相关内容，他们很在行。詹·塞斯基拉，对不起詹，如果我把你的名字读错了。Max Borges Agency在面向消费者的产品方面很出色。格雷格·德尔曼，他在旧金山，经营着一家名为G3 Media的精品公司，专注于科技初创企业领域，他对这个领域非常熟悉。格雷格，我会通过他找到合适的撰稿人，因为他人脉很广。我最近给他发短信说，我需要写一篇关于特定AI技术的文章。他恰好在TechCrunch Disrupt活动上，就帮我联系到了自由撰稿人。太棒了。以上就是四个推荐。我还能再提供更多信息，方便你写进节目笔记里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. This is really useful. If any come to mind as we're chatting, feel free to shout them out again. Similar question, when people are thinking about publications to go after, say you're a startup founder. Is there a list you could just share of just like, here's probably the top five, 10 that you should be thinking about? The obvious ones, you talked about entrepreneur, [inaudible 00:36:15] Company, TechCrunch obviously comes to mind. Is there others that are just like, "Here's a good list to start with?"
turns.zh: 太好了。没问题。这真的很有用。如果在聊天的过程中又想起其他人，也欢迎随时提出来。类似的问题是，当人们考虑合作的媒体平台时，比如初创公司创始人，能否推荐一个入门级别的榜单？比如前五名或前十名值得关注的媒体？像你提到的Entrepreneur、[音频不清晰 00:36:15] Company、TechCrunch这些显而易见的选择。还有其他值得推荐的媒体吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Honestly, it really, so much depends upon what it is that you're looking to do. You could be a startup, founder and entrepreneur and Inc and Fast Company are for maybe some good reason not at the top of your list because you're a startup founder, but your goal right now is to reach consumers. And those publications don't reach consumers and they don't reach people who are in a buying mindset. They reach people who are in a creating mindset. So I would expect that if you have a startup and that startup is not B2B in some way, that it would be possibly very reasonable that business publications might not be your target right now. Maybe Men's Health is. Maybe, I don't know, anything could be. I think oftentimes people tend to think too close to them about where they belong. Lenny, here's a real kind of exchange that happens, which is if somebody will email me, I don't respond to every publicist. (00:37:23): It's just literally not possible. I would not have enough time in the day. I do do my best to respond to every entrepreneur who reaches out because I feel like they deserve a response. And sometimes somebody will email me and they'll send me something and it's just not relevant. And I'll reply and I'll just say, "Hey, thanks. Congratulations on what you've built. But this isn't a fit for entrepreneur." And maybe once a month somebody responds really in a testy way, and they're like, "But don't you write about entrepreneurs? I'm a great entrepreneur success story." It's like, no, that's not what we do. Yes, entrepreneurs are featured in our stories, but no, we're not just a directory of entrepreneurs. Here's a good way of thinking about it. If you have a startup and you're trying to figure out what publications to be in, go look at where your competitors have been featured. That's a great place to start. What audiences are they reaching and how are they doing it? That should give you some direction about where you might want to go next.
turns.zh: 老实说，这真的取决于你想做什么。如果你是一家初创公司、创始人或企业家，或许《Inc》和《Fast Company》并不在你的优先考虑名单上，因为你是一名初创公司创始人，但你现在的目标是触达消费者。而这些刊物并不能触达消费者，也无法触达处于购买模式的人群——它们针对的是处于创造模式的人群。所以我认为，如果你有一家初创公司，而且这家公司并非B2B模式，那么商业类刊物可能目前并非你的目标读者群。或许《Men's Health》更合适。说不定，任何其他媒体都行。我觉得人们往往会过于局限地认为自己应该投稿于特定媒体。莱尼，这里有个真实的交流案例：如果有人给我发邮件，我不会回复每一位公关人员。（00:37:23）这根本不现实，我一天的时间根本不够。我会尽力回复每位联系我的创业者，因为我觉得他们值得得到回应。有时有人会发邮件给我，发送一些不相关的资料。我会回复他们：“嘿，谢谢。祝贺你所取得的成就。但这不适合《Entrepreneur》。”然后可能每月都会有人不耐烦地回击：“但你们不是写创业者的吗？我可是成功的创业典范。”我会回应：“不，我们不只是创业者名录。是的，我们的报道会涉及创业者，但我们不只是一个创业者名录。” 一个好的思路是，如果你有一家初创公司，正在寻找适合投稿的媒体，可以看看你的竞争对手曾在哪些媒体上亮相。这会为你指明下一步的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome advice. On TechCrunch, do you have a perspective on is it worth investing in getting featured in TechCrunch?
turns.zh: 很棒的建议。关于TechCrunch，你觉得在TechCrunch上获得报道是否值得投资？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: I'll tell you a sort of personal press journey moment, and then I think that it will translate into the answer for TechCrunch.
turns.zh: 我给你讲一个我个人的媒体推广经历，然后我觉得这能转化为对TechCrunch的回答。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Okay. Something we haven't talked about so far yet is, and this is sort of almost skipping all the steps that we've laid out to what happens after you get the press. But the point of the press is sometimes to reach the people who are reading it. You get covered in Entrepreneur and entrepreneurs are going to read it and maybe something good will come of it. But sometimes the point of it is not to reach the people who are reading it at all. Possibly a very small number of people are going to read it, which by the way is a real, real possibility. Because although all of these publications that I have mentioned, Entrepreneur, Forbes, Fortune Inc, Fast Company, whatever, these are reaching millions of people, their websites get many, many, many millions of unique visitors each month. That does not mean that your story is going to be read by millions of people. (00:39:40): In fact, the largest possibility here is that your story will reach five to 10,000 people, a small number of people because these publications are publishing tons of stuff. So you might get this story, it might look awesome, it might not reach that many people. That might also be okay. Because maybe the reason in your logic for why to get that kind of coverage is not to have reached that publication's audience at all anyway. Maybe what it really is is to tweet it and then put some money behind promoting that tweet because then you can target that you got coverage to the people who you want to notice you got coverage. (00:40:21): And I see a lot of people do that. They'll take articles that we ran on Entrepreneur and they'll basically turn them into advertisements. And that's really smart because what they got out of Entrepreneur was the social cachet. It was the validation in the marketplace. And then they're going to do something with that themselves. That's really smart. You also see it sometimes the reason to get coverage, it's just so you can put it on your website. As seen in. As seen in is probably more valuable than anyone actually reading that story to begin with. They probably won't read the story. You might not even have to link it on the website. But you could just get to say as seen in. Because again, it gives you that validation. (00:40:56): Me personally, I am building a small podcast company with my friend Nicole Lapin. Nicole Lapin is a bestselling business money expert. And we have a company, she's the founder and I'm an advisor. And it's called Money News Network. We have a podcast on it called Help Wanted that we co-host together. And we got coverage in Variety. And that was the result of pounding on a lot of doors and finally getting someone at Variety to take interest and they ran an article about us. Did we get anything from that story in Variety? The answer is no, like nothing. But you better believe that every email we send out to every potential advertiser, to every partner, includes the link. Variety has covered us. And I guarantee that when someone receives that email, it makes them pay more attention. (00:41:52): And I have used it many times too when I reach out to people. It just gives you that validation. So sometimes what you're looking for is a prize to walk around with. And I would bet that the same is true for TechCrunch, which was your original question. Why get the funding announcement in TechCrunch? Probably not because anyone's going to care because they read it on TechCrunch, but now you can use that to your own means. And sometimes that's more valuable than the press itself.
turns.zh:
好的。到目前为止，我们还没有讨论过一个问题——虽然这有点跳过我们之前铺垫的所有步骤，直接讲媒体报道后的后续。但媒体报道的目的有时并不是为了让读者看到。例如，当你在《Entrepreneur》杂志上获得报道时，读者或许会看到，但实际效果可能微乎其微。这是真实存在的可能性，因为虽然《Entrepreneur》等媒体确实能覆盖数百万读者，每月吸引数亿独立访客，但你的报道未必能触达所有读者。

（00:39:40）事实上，最常见的情况是你的报道只会被5到1万人看到——这毕竟只是个小数目，因为这些媒体每天发布大量内容。所以即便你的报道看起来很棒，也未必能获得大量曝光。但这或许也可以接受，因为你寻求媒体报道的真正目的，或许根本不是让读者看到，而是通过社交媒体推广。比如，你可以在推特上发布报道，并为推广付费，这样就能精准触达目标受众。

（00:40:21）我观察到很多人会这样做。他们会把我们在《Entrepreneur》上发表的文章，包装成广告。这很明智，因为媒体报道带来的社会认可度和市场认可度，本身就足以为他们创造价值。还有些人获取报道只是为了放在自己的网站上。但归根结底，真正有价值的不是报道本身，而是社交媒体上的曝光。

（00:40:56）就我个人而言，我和朋友妮可·拉平（Nicole Lapin）正在创办一家小型播客公司。妮可是畅销商业理财专家，我们共同创立了Money News Network。她是创始人，我是顾问。我们合作推出的播客《Help Wanted》在《Variety》上获得了报道。这得益于我们多次拜访，最终让《Variety》记者对我们感兴趣并撰写报道。那这篇报道对我们有什么实际价值吗？答案是零。但请相信，我们发送给每个潜在广告商和合作伙伴的邮件中，都会附上《Variety》的报道链接。一旦对方收到邮件，关注度必定会提升。

（00:41:52）我在联系别人时也多次使用了这个策略。这能为你赢得认可。有时候，你所追寻的不过是一个可以炫耀的奖杯。我敢打赌，TechCrunch的情况也是如此——这正是你最初的问题所在。为什么要在TechCrunch上发布融资公告？很可能不是因为读者会因此关注，而是你可以利用这个平台为自己服务。有时候，这比媒体报道本身更有价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an awesome insight. It also makes you realize you may not feel like it was a success after spending all this time getting in a story and entrepreneurs. Like, oh, nothing happened. But the benefits may come later, like weeks, months, years later when you start to share that.
turns.zh: 真是深刻的见解。这也让你意识到，花了那么多时间参与故事创作和创业后，你可能并不觉得自己取得了成功。比如，哦，什么事都没发生。但好处或许会迟来几周、几个月甚至几年之久，当你开始分享这些经历时。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Exactly right. A lot of this is what you make of it.
turns.zh: 说得太对了。很多时候，这完全取决于你如何看待它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay. That was extremely interesting. Okay, let's talk about step two. So initially you prepped, we talked about how to think about who to go after and the mission and goals. Then you get to step two, which just figure out who to reach out to at a publication.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的。这真是非常有趣。好的，我们来谈谈第二步。首先你要做好准备，我们讨论了如何思考目标读者、使命和目标。然后进入第二步，就是确定向哪家媒体机构进行推广。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Right. So a lot of people make the mistake of emailing me. If they want coverage in Entrepreneur, they email me. And I understand why they're emailing me. It's really for two reasons. One, I'm the most visible editorial person at Entrepreneur. And so it's easy to find me, it's easy to find my email address. And also they just assume, well, editor in chief, making all the decisions. But no. I mean, think about it. If you have a problem with a purchase that you made on Amazon, you don't email Bezos. He's too busy. And I am not comparing myself to Bezos. But I am the busiest editorial guy at Entrepreneur for whatever the hell that's worth. And I'm just not the guy to pitch because my job actually isn't really to select stories that go in the magazine. My job is to work with editors who develop their own ideas and then I get to say, "Oh, that's a good one," or, "Oh, let's refine that." I'm not sourcing as much. And so you really should start by looking at who's writing about your subject area. (00:43:57): And you can do that by going to the website and surfing around. You can do that by Googling around. But you'll find the answer. Every publication is structured differently. Some people have specific beats. Some publications will be like, "This is the person on the transportation beat." And some publications don't. Entrepreneur doesn't really have a beat system necessarily. But if you look, you'll figure it out. "Oh, that editor is clearly interested in food. That writer is clearly interested in food. They seem to write all the food stories." And a good way, again, to do it is to start with the publication and then look at how they're covering your competitors. So a good example is I was once consulting with a guy who has a kind of fun peanut butter company. It's like imagine peanut butter meets Ben and Jerry's, so it's like peanut butter with lots of stuff and fun names. And so he's trying to figure out how to get press. And originally his thinking, the reason why he reached out to me was because he's like, "Well, I'm an entrepreneur. I run a business. I should be in Entrepreneur." (00:45:05): I was like, "No, no, no, you shouldn't because none of our readers are going to buy your peanut butter. So who is your target audience? Who's buying your stuff?" And he says, "Millennial moms." I said, "Great. Okay, so Cosmo is a good place to reach them. So let's look at how Cosmo covers snacks." I don't know how they cover snacks. I don't read Cosmo, but let's find out. It's not hard. I went to cosmopolitan.com, searched for snacks. What I found immediately was a lot of stories that are all basically roundup-y and anchored to some time-sensitive things. So it's 10 snacks for Valentine's Day, it's our 10 favorite new fall snacks, whatever. It's all stuff like that. So now we know they are not going to run a thousand word feature on your peanut butter company. Instead, the best that you could hope to do is get into one of these seasonal-ish roundups. (00:45:59): So now next step, who's writing these things? Let's look. Let's open some of the articles. The byline is right there. You can click on the byline. You can see what this person does. And in many cases, maybe they're the food editor, maybe they're the lifestyle editor, whatever. You'll see what they cover. And you'll have a good understanding of now how to frame the thing that you're looking for. Now, let me introduce one other possible option. They don't work for the publication at all. They're a freelancer. Publications use a lot of freelancers. Freelancers are basically independent contractors. They're writers who are working sometimes. Sometimes they have longer term deals with publications. Sometimes it's just one-off. My wife is a freelancer. My wife is a freelancer who writes a lot for the New York Times and Washington Post and Guardian. And the interesting thing about my wife versus me is that my wife, whose name is Jen Miller, just so I don't keep saying my wife. (00:46:58): So Jen, on a day-to-day basis as a freelancer is hungrier for stories than me because Jen has to hustle for her food. Jen has to find stories and pitch those stories to editors at publications, and that's when she gets paid. So she actually is more incentivized to be looking for stories than I am because I am a salaried employee of Entrepreneur Magazine. And my email address is very easily found and people just send me stuff all the time. And I should add here also, note that a good journalist, a good writer is not actually sitting around thinking that their job is to wait for people to pitch them so that they can just write about the best pitches. Their job as they see it, is to go and find the most useful things for their audience. And they like to do a lot of that themselves. So they're not sitting around just waiting for your pitches. And in fact, your pitches have to overcome their instinct to go find things themselves. (00:48:02): So Jen is constantly hustling. Jen is constantly talking to people. Jen is curious about the world and will spend a lot of time hunting things down. But if somebody reads a story that she wrote and says, "Ah, I think I have an idea of what this person is interested in," and then tracks her email address down and then emails her, Jen is getting a lot fewer pitches than me, the chances of her reading it are close to a hundred percent. And the chances of her taking it seriously if it's relevant to any of the publications that she writes for is much higher than me. So sometimes going to the staff person is not actually your best move. Finding the freelancer who's doing the work is sometimes the better move.

好的。很多人都会犯一个错误，就是给我发邮件。比如，如果他们想在《Entrepreneur》杂志上获得报道，就会给我发邮件。我理解他们这么做的原因，主要有两个。一是，我是《Entrepreneur》杂志最引人注目的编辑人员，所以大家很容易找到我，也容易获取我的邮箱地址。另外，他们可能误以为编辑总监能决定一切。但事实并非如此。想想看，如果你在亚马逊上买到不好的商品，你不会给贝佐斯发邮件吧。他太忙了。我不是在拿自己和贝佐斯比，但我确实是《Entrepreneur》杂志最忙碌的编辑，尽管这话听起来可能有点自夸。不过我的工作重点并非亲自挑选要发表的稿件，而是与编辑们合作，完善他们的创意提案。比如，“这篇文章不错”，或者“咱们再润色一下”。我不怎么负责挖掘新闻线索。所以大家首先应该去看看谁在报道你的领域。（00:43:57）你可以登录网站浏览相关内容，或者用谷歌搜索相关信息，总之能找到答案。每个出版机构的架构不同，有些有特定报道领域，比如“交通报道专栏”之类的。《Entrepreneur》没有严格的报道分工体系，但通过观察竞争对手的报道方向，你能找到线索。比如我曾为一位经营趣味花生酱公司的客户提供咨询。他的产品理念类似于“花生酱遇上本杰瑞冰淇淋”，即添加多种配料、取有趣名字的花生酱产品。最初他想在《Entrepreneur》上宣传，但我建议他别这么做，因为我们的读者不会买他的花生酱。所以我问：“你的目标读者是谁？谁会购买你的产品？”他回答：“千禧一代的妈妈们。”我说：“很好，那《Cosmo》杂志就是个好选择。看看他们如何报道零食类内容。”我虽然不常读《Cosmo》，但很快发现他们的零食报道都是季节性汇总，比如“情人节十款零食”、“秋季十大热门零食”之类的。所以我们知道他们不会为你的花生酱公司写长篇专题。最佳选择是参与这些季节性汇总报道。

接下来要了解作者信息。打开文章，查看署名作者的背景。很多作者是美食编辑、生活方式编辑等，你能清楚他们的报道方向。这样你就能精准构思你的新闻提案了。最后再说一种可能性——他们根本不为杂志工作，而是自由撰稿人。很多出版机构都大量使用自由撰稿人。
自由撰稿人。他们有时是兼职工作者，有时会与出版机构签订长期合作协议，有时只是临时接活。我妻子就是一名自由撰稿人。她为《纽约时报》、《华盛顿邮报》和《卫报》撰写大量文章。与我相比，她的处境更有挑战性——因为她需要主动争取机会。（00:46:58）所以，简而言之，简作为自由撰稿人，每天都在寻找新闻素材，因为她必须为生计奔波。她需要挖掘新闻线索，并向编辑们推销自己的创意，才有机会获得报酬。而我作为《创业家》杂志的固定员工，邮箱公开，人们随时会给我发送新闻素材。这里需要强调的是，优秀的记者和作家不会被动等待别人来找他们写稿。他们认为自己的职责是主动为读者挖掘最有价值的信息，并且会亲自去做大量调研。因此，他们不会坐等你的新闻提案，相反，你的提案必须突破他们的主动探索欲。（00:48:02）简始终在积极行动。她不断与人沟通，对世界充满好奇，愿意投入大量时间去挖掘新闻。但如果读者读了她的文章后觉得：“啊，我大概能猜到她感兴趣的内容”，然后顺着邮箱找到她并发送提案，那么她收到的提案数量远远少于我，但相关度高的提案被采纳的概率要比我高得多。所以，有时直接联系编辑未必是最佳选择，主动找到正在工作的自由撰稿人，往往更能事半功倍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So many interesting tactical insights that you're sharing. I love it. With this freelancer tip, how do you know they're freelancers? Is there something in the byline?
turns.zh: 您分享的这么多有趣的策略见解，我太喜欢了。关于自由撰稿人的这个技巧，你怎么知道他们是自由撰稿人呢？署名栏里有相关信息吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: If you find them on the publication's website so let's say that you go to Cosmo and you click on a author's bio. If they're staff, it'll say staff. If they're not staff, it'll probably say something else. It might say writer, it might say contributor. It might say Jen Miller is a writer in Brooklyn, New York. But also you can just go one extra step and just Google their name because any smart freelancer has a portfolio website where they should be very easily found.
turns.zh: 如果你在出版物网站上找到他们，比如说你访问Cosmo网站，点击作者简介。如果他们是该刊物的员工，署名栏会显示“员工”。如果不是员工，可能会有其他说明。比如会写“撰稿人”、“供稿人”。比如Jen Miller是纽约布鲁克林的撰稿人。另外，你还可以更进一步，直接在谷歌上搜索他们的名字，因为任何聪明的自由撰稿人都会有个人作品集网站，在那里很容易找到他们。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: So sometimes just take their name, plug it into Google, you'll very quickly figure out who they are.
turns.zh: 所以有时候只需输入他们的名字，搜索一下，很快就能确定他们的身份。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, so let me summarize things that you've taught us so far. One is think about publications that go to people that will buy your thing. So in your example, Cosmo is a good example of someone who would buy this peanut butter thing. Two is don't think of it broad thing. Think about the writer at the thing. So it's not like Cosmo would write about this. It's like, who specifically at Cosmo would write about this? And we find that as go to their site, search for, you talked about search for your competitors, but I think it's even broader, just things related to your area, right? [inaudible 00:50:01].
turns.zh: 好的，我来总结一下你到目前为止教给我们的内容。第一点，要考虑那些可能购买你的内容的出版物。比如在你的例子中，Cosmo就是一个可能购买花生酱相关内容的平台。第二点，不要想得太宽泛，要关注具体的作者。比如Cosmo不会直接报道这个内容，而是要考虑Cosmo内部哪些作者可能对此感兴趣。通过访问他们的网站进行搜索，你提到过搜索竞争对手，但我认为可以更广泛地搜索与你所在领域相关的信息，对吧？[00:50:01的背景音]

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeahs, that;s good point. Search for your category.
turns.zh: 是的，这点很好。搜索你的类别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Even adjacent things probably are close enough. And then this tip about freelancers is really great, that they're hungrier and that they're more likely to respond to your pitch versus someone that's working there. And then also this point that they're like, their assumption is this is not a good pitch and they don't want your pitch. But freelancers have a higher chance of being interested and will pay attention.
turns.zh: 甚至相邻领域的内容也可能足够相关。关于自由撰稿人的这个技巧真的很棒，他们更有上进心，更可能回复你的提案，而不是在职员工。另外，自由撰稿人通常会认为你的提案不够好，不感兴趣。但自由撰稿人更有可能感兴趣并关注。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, freelancers got to eat.
turns.zh: 是啊，自由撰稿人也要养家糊口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Is there anything else along this step of finding somebody at a publication that you want to share?
turns.zh: 太棒了。在寻找出版物作者的这个步骤中，你还有什么其他要分享的技巧吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Well, the next step is going to be how to actually reach out to them and pitch. So at this stage, I think that we've fairly well covered it. And I love your summary. And just to double click on part of that, the reason why you're doing a lot of this is not just for the crazy busy work of it. But it's because you have to understand that the media ... Just sort of go back to translating the media. The media, which is a phrase that is used in all sorts of different ways, is a pretty bad way of actually understanding the media because the "media" makes it feel like it's a unified entity. In politics, the media will be criticized as a sort of multiple publications colluding together in some way. But the way that we're talking about it is just as organizations that you're trying to reach out to. (00:51:25): But really and truly, these are just publishing companies made up of individuals. And those individuals are all making fairly subjective decisions about what it is that they're going to write about. And there are layers of approval that they have to pass through.
