turns.zh: 接下来是她所做的。她的名字，我要特别提一下。她叫梅格·奥哈拉，是一位加拿大风景画家。这又是一个小企业。（01:00:21）她写道："嗨，杰森，我有个故事创意，觉得对你、对《企业家》杂志以及《问题解决者》播客都很有价值。"这是我为《企业家》杂志主持的节目。然后她说："这是我业务近况。所有企业家在新冠疫情期间都必须灵活应变。这是一个关于加拿大一位艺术家如何从边境关闭中获益的故事。"这真让我好奇。哦，具体怎么做呢？（01:00:42）"三月份新冠疫情来袭时，北美所有滑雪场提前关闭。滑雪者在加拿大属于高收入群体，收入位居前5%之列。"（01:00:53）好吧，不管怎样。她接着说。我现在还记得，她告诉我，她原来的业务是受雇于滑雪场，为他们的设施绘制风景画。然而边境关闭后，人们不再去滑雪场，她不得不彻底改变经营方式。（01:01:15）于是她开始思考：既然不能再为滑雪场工作了，他们也不雇用我了。但那些曾在滑雪场工作、见过我作品、或常去滑雪场、对我的作品熟悉的滑雪者，现在也不滑雪了。他们可能正坐在家里，怀念滑雪时光。他们渴望看到自己最爱的滑雪胜地的美景，同时又有闲置资金，因为不再把钱花在滑雪场了。（01:01:39）她用项目符号列出问题与解决方案。我很喜欢这种方式，因为她听过《问题解决者》播客，这个节目正是以这种结构展开的——先说问题，接着说解决方案。她详细阐述了：滑雪者无法前来，人们在家的时间更多了。（01:01:56）解决方案是：我为他们的家创作艺术品，描绘他们曾滑雪时最爱的景色。她滔滔不绝地讲个不停。（01:02:03）读到这里，我觉得这个人重新发明业务的故事很值得分享。当时一个市场关闭，却创造了新市场，这正是人们想听的。因为那时每个人都在思考如何重塑自我和业务。（01:02:21）尽管我接触的多是复杂的大型企业，但有时听一位普通人讲述最简单的事——比如在画布上挥洒颜料——讲述如何为自己重塑事业，真的很美好。因为你能从中提取出许多精彩的小启示，适用于广泛受众。（01:02:44）梅格发来邮件，我回复道："我喜欢这个主意。"然后我们就合作了。这是一个很好的例子，说明有人花时间了解我的工作，甚至注意到我沟通的结构，然后迅速、清晰地向我提交了一个量身定制的提案，并以一种我能想象传达给听众的方式讲述她的故事。（01:03:12）在那一刻，答应合作变得轻而易举。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an amazing example. I just took some notes on things that she did right based on things you've shared in the past. (01:03:19): Even just from the subject line or the first sentence, it was clear that she knew you. She knew you had this podcast, she knew the magazine, and she even expressed this specifically, you're going to be interested in this. She mentioned how this, she has a story. She starts immediately with a story. There's not the value prop of the company, here's what we do and here's why we're awesome. And then the lessons, the mission of Entrepreneur you talked about, is insights and lessons that people achieve, and she just went straight to here's what we've learned.
turns.zh: 真是个绝佳的案例。我刚刚根据你过去分享的信息，记录了她做得好的几个方面。（01:03:19）：即使仅从邮件主题或开头第一句就能明显看出，她很了解你。她知道你有这个播客，了解《企业家》杂志，甚至特别强调“你会对此感兴趣”。她提到自己有故事可讲，直接以故事开场。没有那种“我们公司很棒”的宣传话术，也没有那种“我们能提供什么价值”的说辞。她直接切入主题，讲述自己学到的经验教训，传递《企业家》杂志所倡导的理念——帮助人们从成功中汲取智慧。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I could see why that resonated.
turns.zh: 所以我能理解为什么这能引起共鸣。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, it was great. And the next thing that made it a real success, by the way for her, was that once I got her on the phone, she was, and I find this, this is a make or break thing for me. Because I can talk to somebody and then kill the story, or not run the podcast. She was willing to be open about challenges. (01:04:17): I mean, she had reached out because of challenges, but not everyone is. I will get a pitch from someone who is presenting like, oh, we had this challenge in the business. But then when I talk to them, they act as if there was no problem. Or the problem was really small and their ingenuity immediately made this a very successful business. And that's not interesting to me. (01:04:42): Because success stories are not interesting. They're not interesting to anybody. It's not useful for you to just hear that someone else succeeded. What's useful is for you to hear how someone else faced challenges that you faced. And got through them so that you can see. Aha, that's an interesting strategy to use for me. (01:05:01): I hate success stories. I love problem solving stories. And that's why when I talk to an entrepreneur, I expect them to be really open about that stuff. And if they're not, I basically lose interest.
turns.zh: 确实很棒。顺便说一句，对她而言，这次成功的关键在于，一旦我和她通上电话，她就非常坦诚地谈论遇到的挑战。我发现这对我来说至关重要。因为我可能和某人交谈，结果却无法把故事讲好，或者无法推进播客项目。他们不愿坦然面对挑战。（01:04:17）：我的意思是，她主动联系我是因为遇到了挑战，但并非所有人都如此。我曾收到过某人的提案，他们声称在业务中遇到过挑战。但当我与他们交谈时，他们却表现得好像根本没有问题存在。或者问题微不足道，凭借自己的智慧就轻松把业务做得很成功。这对我来说毫无意义。（01:04:42）：因为成功故事并无趣味性。对任何人来说都不具吸引力。听别人讲述别人的成功故事毫无用处。真正有价值的，是听别人如何直面你所面临的挑战，并成功克服它们，这样你就能意识到，啊，这对我来说是个不错的策略。（01:05:01）：我讨厌成功故事。我喜欢解决问题的故事。这就是为什么与创业者交流时，我期望他们能坦诚面对这些挑战。如果他们不愿如此，我基本上就失去兴趣了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The hero's journey. I'd love to hear another example. But before that, hearing this, obviously it takes a bunch of time to do this for a founder. I guess, two questions. Just, how many places should somebody probably try to reach out to give them a chance of being successful? And then do you have any thoughts on how much time they should put into something like this? I know it's a very broad question. But, any thoughts there?
turns.zh: 英雄之旅。我很想听另一个例子。但在此之前，听了这些内容，很显然，创始人要做好这件事需要投入大量时间。我想问两个问题。首先，一个人大概应该尝试联系多少个地方，才能有成功的机会？然后，对于投入多少时间，你有什么看法？我知道这是个很宽泛的问题。但你有什么想法吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, it's a really broad question. So again, this is in some way why, in a large way, why a lot of people hire PR. Because PR can just move this along. They can reach a lot of people very fast, whereas you as an individual cannot. (01:05:51): One way to think about it is, you're going to be on the hunt. You're going to try to make this work, and you're going to take a couple bets and hope that some of them pay off. (01:06:01): Another way of thinking about it is, this is a passive activity. And I'll spend some time when I'm reading media, thinking about this, kind of developing an idea. Another thing that you can do, follow a bunch of writers and editors on social media. (01:06:20): Meg, I can't remember the order of operations here, because I know that Meg follows me on Instagram now, because she's DMd me many times. And I respond to everybody. I can't remember if she followed me before, but she might've. And maybe she even DMd me a few times. Usually it's somebody's responding to an Instagram story or something. (01:06:38): And I've seen a lot of people use this strategy with me, and I think that it's a really smart one. Which is basically, before you ever pitch, just get me to recognize your name. Just engage in social media in a very casual way, such that when you email me, I think, do I know who that person is? Meg O'Hara, I think I know who that person is. It just makes it more likely that I'll open the email. (01:07:08): And I see a lot of people do that. They'll spend a long time engaging with me on social media before ever pitching me. I know what they're doing, I understand that it's probably calculated. I still like it. It's smart. Because it means that by the time that they've reached out, I think you have a pretty good sense of my work. Which means that what you're bringing to me is probably in pretty good faith. And for that, I like it. It's a good filter. (01:07:36): So if you've been listening to this whole thing, and you're thinking, this is a tremendous amount of work, I have a new product launch, or I have a bunch of budget that I can spend on this, this individual kind of approach, it may not be for you. You might want to just spend a bunch of time instead interviewing different PR firms. And find the one that seems most aligned with and understands your story, and your vision, and knows people in your space shortcuts a lot of this. (01:08:06): But even then, even then, I think that having heard this is really useful. Because at some point, if the PR person is successful, you are going to get on the phone with the writer or editor. And it's very useful to understand how they think. That they're not there to serve you. That this isn't a service that they're providing you. (01:08:27): So you better understand what they're entering into this with, and what they have in mind. When they're asking you questions, they're asking questions, thinking, this is what my audience is going to be curious about. This is how I'm going to drive this person in this interview towards the kinds of insights that my audience are going to find gratifying. (01:08:44): So the more that you understand who you're dealing with, the better.
turns.zh:
是啊，这确实是个很宽泛的问题。所以再说一次，这就是为什么从宏观层面来看，很多人会聘请公关公司的原因。因为公关公司能推动事情进展。他们能迅速触达大量受众，而个人却做不到这一点。（01:05:51）：你可以这样想：你得主动出击，努力促成合作，尝试几次尝试，希望其中一些能成功。（01:06:01）：另一种思路是，这是一种被动的策略。当我阅读媒体内容时，我会思考这个问题，逐步构思一个创意。还有一个方法，就是在社交媒体上关注大量作家和编辑。（01:06:20）：梅格，我记不清这里的操作顺序了，因为我知道她现在在Instagram上关注我了，因为她多次给我发私信。我回复了所有人。不记得她之前是否关注过我，但她可能关注过，甚至给我发过几次私信。通常是有人回复了我的Instagram动态之类的。（01:06:38）：我见过很多人用这种策略。他们在联系我之前，先让我记住你的名字。以一种非常随意的方式参与社交媒体，这样当你给我发邮件时，我会想，我认识这个人吗？梅格·奥哈拉，我觉得我认识她。这就大大增加了我打开邮件的可能性。

（01:07:08）：我看到很多人这么做。他们会在联系我之前，先在社交媒体上与我互动很久。我知道他们这么做是有意为之的，我理解这很可能是经过深思熟虑的。但我还是很欣赏这种做法，因为这意味着当他们联系我时，我已经对你的工作有了相当深入的了解。这意味着你带给我的内容很可能是真诚的。为此，我很欣赏。这是一个很好的过滤机制。

（01:07:36）：如果你听完了整个讨论，觉得这工作量太大，我有新产品要发布，或者有大量预算可以投入，这种个性化的方法可能不适合你。你或许更愿意花时间面试不同的公关公司。找到最贴合你的故事、愿景、并了解你所在领域的人脉的公司，能省去很多麻烦。

（01:08:06）：但即便如此，听完这些还是很有帮助的。因为如果公关人员成功了，最终你还是要和记者或编辑通电话。了解他们的思维方式非常重要。他们不是为你服务的，这不是他们提供的服务。

（01:08:27）：所以你最好理解他们的立场和意图。当他们问你问题时，他们是在思考：我的读者会对这个感兴趣吗？我要如何引导采访对象提供读者会觉得有价值的见解？

（01:08:44）：所以你对合作对象了解得越多越好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And also just having done it yourself, you'll better understand what to ask your folks, how they're going to work, find opportunities to improve the way they're operating. On that question of quantity, say you're doing this, say you're spending the time. I'm going to really invest in understanding Jason and whoever else. (01:09:05): Is there a rule of thumb you'd recommend? Try to do this for three publications to get one, or is it five? I don't know. Is there anything there that you could recommend?
turns.zh: 另外，当你亲自做过这些事后，你会更清楚该如何向团队成员提问，他们将如何开展工作，如何寻找改进运营方式的机会。关于数量的问题，假设你正在做这件事，并且投入了大量时间。我会真正投入精力去了解杰森以及其他相关人员。（01:09:05）：你有什么推荐的经验法则吗？比如尝试向三家媒体投稿才能获得一篇报道，还是五家？我不知道。你能给些建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: So it's really dependent upon how easy you are to write about. I may just sort of note, if you are some kind of B2B service, especially in some kind of very niche or wonky space, it's going to be really hard for you to get [inaudible 01:09:40]. So hard that it might actually not even be worth trying. Because there are other things that you can do, or things that we haven't even talked about yet. (01:09:46): You could say, you know what? Screw it. I'm not going to try to get coverage for my company. Why don't I just try to position myself as an expert? Right? It's a totally different kind of approach. Where instead, what you're maybe trying to do is just hook onto the news, try to get a quote or a perspective to a reporter who might be writing about something. I get these all the time. (01:10:07): Something breaks, some news breaks, and people start reaching out to me. And they'll say, "This just happened in the news. And my client," or sometimes just the individual, "I have this insight into this, and here's what I would say if you want to interview me." (01:10:22): It's not going to be a feature about you, You're not going to be the subject, there's no photo of you. You might get a quote. You might get a quote in a story. Which again, is all you need to be able to say as featured in on your website. So that's the reason why people do that. (01:10:33): So sometimes it's about that. Sometimes it's about you could just be a writer. You might try to just pitch authoritative articles by you to different publications. Get yourself out in that way. Sometimes, again, you're not going to be able to be easily written about. And sometimes you are. Sometimes you made some insane technology that everyone's going to be talking about, and it's going to be super easy for you to get press. (01:10:56): At which point your hit rate is going to be much higher. That's why going into this with really realistic expectations, and if you're going to work with PR, having PR who can set and hold you to those realistic expectations, can just save you a lot of heartache.
turns.zh: 这实际上取决于你是否容易被报道。如果你提供的是B2B服务，特别是某个非常小众或复杂的领域，要获得报道会非常困难。困难到可能根本不值得尝试，因为还有其他你可以做的事情，或者我们还没有讨论过的方法。（01:09:46）：你可以说，管他的，我就不试图为我的公司争取报道了。为什么不试着把自己定位成专家呢？对吧？这是一种完全不同的方法。相反，你可能只是想紧跟新闻动态，试图向可能正在撰写相关内容的记者提供引语或观点。这种情况我经常遇到。（01:10:07）：有突发新闻时，人们会联系我。他们会说：“新闻里刚发生了这个事儿。我的客户”——或者有时只是个人——“我对此有这样的见解，如果你想采访我的话。”（01:10:22）：报道不会以你为主角，也不会有你的照片。你可能会获得引语。你的引语可能会出现在报道中。同样，这足以让你在自己的网站上宣称被媒体报道过。这就是人们这样做的原因。（01:10:33）：所以有时就是这样。有时你可以自己写作。你可以尝试向不同媒体投稿权威文章，通过这种方式崭露头角。有时，相反，你可能很难被轻松报道。但有时你又能做到。有时你开发了某项令人惊叹的技术，人人都在谈论，那你就很容易获得媒体关注。（01:10:56）：这种情况下，你的成功率会高得多。这就是为什么要抱着现实的期望去开展这项工作，如果你要与公关公司合作，确保公关公司能设定并督促你达成这些现实期望，这能为你省去很多烦恼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along the same lines, there's always this idea of exclusivity and people want to write first about a thing. Say you talked about an awesome technology. Do you have advice on, do you just pitch the same thing to all of them and hope they all write about it? Do you pitch them different stories? Do you offer one an exclusive, any advice there?
turns.zh: 同样，总是存在独家报道的概念，人们希望先报道某个新闻。假设你谈论了一项很棒的技术。你对此有建议吗？你是向所有媒体投稿相同的内容，希望他们都报道，还是向不同媒体投稿不同的故事？你会提供独家报道吗？有任何建议吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Everyone has a different approach to this. The number one rule here is just, don't do it in a way that the people in media feel like you're playing them. Because they won't have tolerance for it. I would rather walk away from something like this than do some funny dance with somebody. (01:11:48): So my favorite version of this goes like this. Actually, there's a founder who recently, I met him years ago. So when he reached out, I recognized the name immediately. And he reached out and he's like, hey, we did this really interesting thing and we haven't told anybody about it yet. And I'd love to see if it's a fit for entrepreneurs. (01:12:10): So I hop on the phone with him, and he tells me. And I'm not going to tell you what it's yet because we haven't run the story. But after 15, 20 minutes, I say, yeah, you know what? This is a really interesting story. (01:12:20): And frankly, I know other media outlets are going to be interested in this too, particularly because a finance element to it. So I think the Wall Street Journal, and Bloomberg, and those kinds of places are going to be interested in this. (01:12:32): He wants to go to Entrepreneur for whatever reasons he wants. I mean, I think probably two. Because number one, he wants to position himself towards that audience. And then number two, there's a trust factor. He knows me in a way that he doesn't know the editors over there. And so he feels like I'll probably treat the story more carefully. (01:12:49): So we worked out a deal, which he proposed. And the deal is that we'll get the exclusive, and there's going to be a three-hour window after our story runs, and then they're going to start responding to everyone else. And then they're going to start talking to other people, or maybe they'll even line it up and reach out to some other media. (01:13:10): And that's fine with me. I understand. And we're going to create a little embargo window. And we'll go first, and then they're going to talk to everybody else. (01:13:21): Sometimes you can offer an exclusive to someone in that you are going to release the news to everybody, but only one media outlet is going to get the interview. Which works really well if you have a big personality. (01:13:35): So for example, recently a company that Mark Cuban has invested in offered us that, right? They're like, we have this news. We're going to reach out, we're going to send the news everywhere, but we're going to give you the exclusive interview with Mark Cuban. He's going to do one interview and he'll do it with you. You can parse it out in any way. You just want everyone to feel like you're being upfront with them.
turns.zh: 每个人对此都有不同的处理方式。这里的首要原则就是，别让媒体觉得你在耍他们。他们可容忍不了这种行为。我宁愿放弃这样的机会，也不愿和别人虚与委蛇。（01:11:48）：我最喜欢的案例是这样的。有个创始人，我几年前就认识他了。他联系我时，我立刻认出了他的名字。他说，你们做了一件很有趣的事，还没告诉任何人，我想看看这对创业者是否有吸引力。（01:12:10）：我和他通了电话，他告诉我这个项目。但因为还没正式报道，我现在不能透露具体内容。聊了15、20分钟后，我说，这故事确实很有意思。（01:12:20）：坦白说，我知道其他媒体也会感兴趣，尤其是涉及金融元素的部分。《华尔街日报》、彭博社之类的媒体肯定会关注。（01:12:32）：他想把稿子卖给《创业家》杂志，可能有两个原因。一是想定位目标读者；二是信任因素。他了解我，却不了解那边的编辑，所以觉得我会更谨慎处理稿件。（01:12:49）：我们达成了协议。他提议我们独家报道，在报道发布后的三小时内不回应其他媒体，然后再和其他人沟通。（01:13:10）：我完全理解这种做法。我们会先独家发布，再让他们和其他媒体合作。（01:13:21）：有时你可以提供独家报道，但只让一家媒体采访。比如马克·库班投资的公司就这么做，他们说我们有独家新闻，先给你们独家采访，之后再发给其他媒体。只要你人缘好，这种做法效果不错。（01:13:35）：比如最近马克·库班投资的一家公司就找我们合作，他们说我们有独家新闻，先发给你们，但马克只接受你们的采访。你们可以自由编排，但要确保信息真实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that they're getting something special, as much as possible. That makes sense. (01:14:02): You touched on this relationship piece, and that's something I wanted to ask. It feels like in tech, a lot of reporters end up writing a negative story, because a lot of times that's what people want to read. Why is this destroying the world? (01:14:14): I actually had a fast company do a thing on me, and I talked to the reporter, and I had no idea. Was he going to just completely tear me apart, or is he going to be really friendly and positive over what I'm doing? And I have no idea, and it just comes out. (01:14:24): It's not like I look at it before it comes out. So do you have any just advice to give you a set, help if this is going to turn into something positive or negative? I know you have no idea
turns.zh: 尽可能让他们觉得自己获得了特别待遇。这很合理。（01:14:02）：你提到了这种合作关系，我正想问这个问题。在科技领域，许多记者最后写出负面报道，因为这往往是读者想看的内容。为什么这会毁掉世界？（01:14:14）：实际上《快公司》曾对我做过报道，我和记者聊天，完全不知道他会不会把我批得体无完肤，还是会友好积极地报道我的工作。完全不知道，内容就这么发出来了。（01:14:24）：我又没机会提前看稿子。所以你有没有什么建议，能帮助判断这会是正面还是负面报道？我知道你也不知道。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: What happened, by the way? Was it positive or negative?
turns.zh: 顺便问一下发生了什么？是好是坏？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super-positive.
turns.zh: 非常积极。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Great.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was very happy with it, yeah.
turns.zh: 我对此非常满意，是的。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Okay, good, good. I'm glad to hear that. (01:14:40): So part of it is the publication itself, right? Entrepreneur, and I would say Fast Company, are just sort of not in the business of running negative stories. And the reason is, it doesn't serve our audience. My audience is coming to me to learn things for their business. Tearing somebody apart just doesn't help them in any way. (01:14:59): So part of it is just what ecosystem are you dealing with? You can also look at the past work of the writer. And if you work with a PR person, it's funny because occasionally somebody has accidentally forwarded this to me, and I'll see the dossier that a PR agency will put together on me. (01:15:17): But a PR agency, if they set you up with an interview with someone, they'll usually do some digging. And they'll find, what does this person usually write about? What kind of stories do they do? What are they generally interested in? So you can have a sense, right? What kind kind of thing are they doing? (01:15:33): And past that, there's also a question of, well, what are you doing in the world, right? I mean, if there is something somewhat controversial about you, and especially if you're engaging with an outlet that is interested in that kind of stuff, there's a halfway-decent chance they're at least going to explore it with you, and ask you about it. And if you're weird and cagey with them, they're going to think that there's more to it, and they're going to start digging more. (01:16:03): But the ultimate answer here is that every part of this, and this has come through, I'm sure, in our whole conversation, every part of this process is really out of your control. Does somebody pay attention to you? What do they write about you? When do they write about? All of it is outside of your control, (01:16:23): Which again, is the reason why it's not smart to think about press as a primary strategy for driving growth. It's a good add-on, but these people are going to do what they're going to do. And the best you can do is read the tea leaves.
turns.zh: 好的，好的。很高兴听到这个消息。（01:14:40）：所以部分原因在于出版物本身，对吧？《Entrepreneur》杂志，还有《Fast Company》，他们的业务模式不适合报道负面新闻。原因是这对我们的读者没有好处。我读者来找我是为了学习商业知识的，而把别人贬低一通对他们毫无帮助。（01:14:59）：所以部分原因在于你所处的生态环境如何？你也可以看看作者过去的作品。如果你和公关人员合作，有趣的是，有时候有人会不小心把资料转发给我，我就能看到公关公司为我整理的档案。（01:15:17）：但公关公司如果帮你安排采访，他们通常会做一些调查。他们会了解这个人通常写什么内容？他们做什么样的报道？他们对什么感兴趣？这样你就能有所了解，对吧？他们在做什么样的事情？（01:15:33）：除此之外，还有一个问题，那就是，你在世上做什么呢？我的意思是，如果你有一些比较有争议的地方，特别是当你与对此感兴趣的媒体合作时，他们很有可能会和你探讨这个问题，并询问你的看法。如果你对他们遮遮掩掩，他们会觉得事情另有隐情，就会进一步调查。（01:16:03）：但最终的答案是，这一切，每个部分，我相信在我们的整个对话中都已经提到了——这个过程的每一步都完全超出你的控制。有人关注你吗？他们写些什么？什么时候写？这一切都超出你的控制。（01:16:23）这就是为什么把媒体作为推动增长的主要策略是不明智的。这是一个不错的补充，但这些人会按他们的方式行事。而你能做的最好的事情就是解读他们的暗示。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It was a very weird ... I don't get press often, it's not like something I pursue. But it was just like, this is wild. I'm just going to talk to this guy, and then something will come out. I have no idea what it might be. (01:16:46): He might have things wrong, because I didn't get a chance to review, and might skew things. But it's a strange experience to go through. But it all worked out great.
turns.zh: 是的。这真的很奇怪……我不常接受媒体采访，这不是我主动追求的。但就是这样，太不可思议了。我只是要和那个人聊聊，然后就会有消息传出来。完全不知道会是什么结果。（01:16:46）：他可能理解有误，因为我没有机会校对，可能会把事情搞砸。但这确实是一次奇特的经历。不过结果都很棒。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, it is. It's very strange. (01:16:58): It is, it's strange. And I find that people often don't ... In business, people understand the structure of what's happening. They understand that we're a business magazine, we're going to write a story about a business. It's going to take a certain form. (01:17:14): But I've done a lot of different writing, and I have had the experience many times over my career where I will spend a lot of time with people, and they will have really no understanding of what it is that I'm doing at all. They can't conceptualize it. (01:17:30): And then the story will come out and then they'll always reach out to me and they'll be like, oh, now I finally understand what you were even trying to do. It's fascinating. (01:17:40): It is a vulnerable experience, and you have to know that. And the more you try to control it, the more the reporter is going to be annoyed at you. And the more, in fact, the reporter might try to take a shot at you in the story as a result. Because they found you too controlling, because they felt like you...
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。这太奇怪了。（01:16:58）：确实如此，确实很奇怪。我发现人们往往不明白……在商业领域，人们能理解事物的结构。他们知道我们是一家商业杂志，要写关于商业的报道。文章会遵循一定的格式。（01:17:14）：但我做过很多不同类型的写作，在我的职业生涯中多次遇到这样的情况：我会花大量时间与人们交流，而他们根本不理解我在做什么。他们无法理解其中的逻辑。（01:17:30）：然后文章发表后，他们总会联系我，说哦，现在我终于明白你想做什么了。这真是令人着迷。（01:17:40）：这是一种脆弱的体验，你必须清楚这一点。你越试图控制局面，记者就会越反感你，甚至可能在报道中故意针对你。因为他们觉得你控制欲太强，因为他们觉得你……

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: They found you too controlling because they felt like you had something to hide. This is not a comfortable thing. You have to go into this being vulnerable and you have to know that there's a chance that it could blow up in your face. That's the price that you're paying for reaching their audience.
turns.zh: 他们觉得你控制欲太强，因为他们觉得你有不可告人的秘密。这可不是件舒服的事。你必须以脆弱的心态去面对这种情况，而且你要知道事情可能会失控。这就是你要为触达读者群体而付出的代价。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Great advice. How about we do just one more example of an awesome email pitch that you got and then we get to our very exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 很棒的建议。我们再举一个你成功获得的精彩邮件提案案例，然后就进入我们激动人心的闪电问答环节吧。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: I'll tell you about a pitch. I don't know that I have it in my inbox still, do I? No, it's not there, sadly. I'll just tell you about it.
turns.zh: 我给你们讲一个提案。我不知道邮箱里还有没有这份提案？不，恐怕没有了。我就简单讲一下吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Ii leads to something that is another way of thinking about getting press, which I think is really important for people to remember. So far, Lenny, we've spent the majority of our time talking about press in the form of some kind of feature on you, writing about you or including you in some kind of prominent way in a story that's basically highlighting the thing that you wanted to get out there, your product or something about your business, something. Then we talked a little bit about another way of doing it, which is sort of putting you out as an expert in authority. There's another way of thinking about this, which is that you can either create or present context in which you just happen to be a part. (01:19:18): Here's the story pitch that I got that leads into this. This is years and years and years ago. I had just started at Entrepreneur. I hear from a guy named Fred Ruckel. Fred Ruckel has got a cat toy and it's called the Ripple Rug. It's basically, imagine a rug and then another rug kind on top of it, but ill-suited. The rug is lumpy, there's a lot of lumps in and there are holes. This is for a cat to kind of crawl in and out these spaces and bat and do whatever cats do. I don't know. I don't know a cat. He wanted to tell me about the sales of this Ripple Rug and about how the sales are skyrocketing and all the things that he thought made it special. It's made out of recycled bottles and whatever the stuff, made in the USA, all cool stuff, but not relevant to me because we're not cat toy monthly and we're not reaching a whole bunch of cat owners, not that I know of. (01:20:16): I replied and I said, what I usually say, "Congratulations on what you've built, but it's just not a fit for coverage." Now Fred stumbled his way into this, but he did really a very smart thing because what he responded with was he said, "Totally understand. If you're ever interested in learning about a gigantic scam that's happening on Amazon and eBay that we've been caught up in, let me know." I was like, "Oh, well, yeah, I guess I am interested in hearing about that." I said, "Tell me more." He sent me this long email. Fred loves long emails, and I got him on the phone and had him explain, and finally I understood it. (01:20:53): This is, and maybe people are familiar with this, but this is sort of known as Amazon to eBay arbitrage. Basically the idea here is that Fred is selling his Ripple Rug on Amazon, or at least he was then, I don't know if he still is, but he's selling his Ripple Rug on Amazon. There are a lot of people who are copying the listing for his Ripple Rug and making their own postings for it on eBay. They sell it for a slightly higher price. Let's say that, and again, I'm making these up, but let's say the Fred is selling his Ripple Rug for $30 on Amazon, so somebody will sell it for $40 on eBay. Then somebody buys it on eBay, they find it, they buy it on eBay, they pay $40, that person gets $40, takes $30 of it, goes to Amazon, buys the Ripple Rug, and then just has it shipped to the buyer. It's arbitrage. (01:21:47): You might think, "Well, why would Fred care about this? He still gets the sale." The reason he caress about this is because the Ripple Rug shows up at the customer's house and it shows up in a Amazon box, even though they bought it on eBay. They think, "Why did that happen?" Then the next thing they do is they go to Amazon and they discover that it's cheaper on Amazon and now they feel ripped off. Who do they feel like they got ripped off by? Fred, because they don't know about the arbitrage. They don't know that they exist. (01:22:21): This person who has at this point opened the cat toy and probably had their cat roll around in it, now shoves the whole thing back in a box and returns it and Fred gets dinged and that's why he doesn't like this. He has tried and tried and tried to get Amazon and eBay to stop this, but he said, "Nobody seems to care and all these small businesses are losing tons of money on returns because of this." I had never heard of this. I thought it was fascinating. It's like a problem small business owners are dealing with. I was like, "Fred, do you know other people who are dealing with this?" He's like, "Yeah, I talk to them on the line all the time." He sends me off. (01:22:54): I reported this whole thing out. I wrote this three 4,000 word story on this thing, and Fred was the main character because he was the way to understand this problem. I did all the reporting and I contacted the platforms and I contacted the people who make the arbitrage software. I did a whole report, but Fred got his press because sometimes, and here's the lesson, sometimes you are not the story, but you can be part of the story. Sometimes that means if Fred stumbled into it, but I get plenty of people who've reach out and maybe they have a real estate startup and there's something really interesting happening in the real estate space and they reach out and they tell me about this really interesting thing that's happening in the real estate space and the role that they happen to play in it. Now I think, "Oh, well that's interesting. Maybe there's a story about that." (01:23:46): My wife, the freelancer, Jen Miller, she's done this many times where she once did this story about there was a bunch of startups that were all related to helping people prepare for death in some way or another. She's not going to write about one of them, but when somebody reached out and said, "Hey, here's a trend happening and we are one of them." Well, great, that's an interesting story. She wrote that and the company that reached out to her got kind of prominent billing because they were the ones who reached out. You know Barbara Corcoran from Shark Tank?
turns.zh:
这引出了另一种思考获取媒体曝光的方式，我认为这对人们来说非常重要。到目前为止，莱尼，我们大部分时间都在讨论以某种专题报道、新闻报道或突出你的产品或业务的形式获取媒体关注。然后，我们稍微探讨了另一种方法，即将你塑造成权威专家。还有一种思路，那就是你可以创造或呈现一个你恰好身处其中的场景。（01:19:18）：以下是我收到的引出这个话题的提案。这是多年前的事了。我刚加入《Entrepreneur》杂志。收到弗雷德·鲁克尔的邮件。他有个叫“波纹地毯”的宠物玩具。想象一下，一块地毯，上面再叠加另一块，但质地不平整，布满凸起和孔洞。猫咪可以在这些空间里爬进爬出，玩耍。这玩具由回收瓶制成，美国制造，各种酷炫元素，但对我们来说并不相关，因为我们不是宠物玩具类月刊，也接触不到大量猫主人。（01:20:16）：我回复了常见套话：“祝贺你打造的产品，但不适合报道。”弗雷德巧妙回应：“完全理解。如果你对亚马逊和eBay上大规模诈骗感兴趣，我们正深陷其中。”我一听：“哦，好吧，我确实想听听。”他发来长邮件。弗雷德喜欢长邮件，我跟他通话后终于明白了。（01:20:53）：这就是众所周知的亚马逊到eBay套利。基本思路是：弗雷德在亚马逊上销售波纹地毯（当时还在卖，不确定现在是否继续）。有人复制他的listing在eBay上挂牌，标价略高。比如弗雷德在亚马逊卖30美元，eBay卖40美元。买家在eBay买后，发现货源来自亚马逊，产生疑惑，接着去亚马逊发现更便宜，觉得被坑了。谁会觉得被坑？弗雷德，因为买家不知道套利存在。
它们确实存在。（01:22:21）：这个人此前打开了猫咪玩具，可能让猫咪在里面打滚玩耍后，又把整个玩具塞回盒子退货，结果弗雷德被扣了分，这就是他不喜欢这种情况的原因。他反复尝试让亚马逊和eBay停止这种行为，但他说：“似乎没人关心，很多小企业因此在退货上损失惨重。” 我从未听说过这种情况。我觉得这很令人惊讶。这就像小企业主们正在应对的一个问题。我问：“弗雷德，你还认识其他面临这种情况的人吗？” 他说：“是的，我经常和他们通话。” 然后他就挂了电话。（01:22:54）：我报道了整个事件。我写了一篇4000字的报道，把弗雷德作为主角，因为他是理解这个问题的重要人物。我做了所有的调查工作，联系了各大平台和开发套利软件的公司。我完成了整个报道，但弗雷德获得了媒体关注。这里有个启示，有时候你不是新闻的主角，但你可以成为故事的一部分。有时候，弗雷德只是偶然遇到了这个问题，但我也接到过很多人的联系，比如房地产创业公司，他们在房地产领域有很有趣的动态，主动联系我分享他们的故事。现在我会想：“哦，这很有意思，或许可以写成一篇报道。”（01:23:46）：我的自由撰稿人妻子珍·米勒也多次遇到过类似情况。她曾写过一篇关于多个帮助人们为死亡做准备的初创公司的报道。她原本不打算写其中一家，但有人主动联系她说：“嘿，我们这里有个新趋势，我们公司就是其中一员。” 太好了！这就是个有趣的故事。她写了这篇报道后，主动联系她的那家公司因为主动发声而获得了显著曝光。你们听说过《创智赢家》里的芭芭拉·科科兰吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think so. I think so.
turns.zh: 我觉得是的。我觉得是的。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah. She's been a regular Shark Tank since the very beginning.
turns.zh: 是啊。她从一开始就是《创智赢家》节目的常驻嘉宾。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: She made her fortune by building a real estate company called Corcoran, realtors, buy and sell property. The way in which she built this company is fascinating. Barbara, before she was Barbara Corcoran of Corcoran Realty, Barbara Corcoran was random New York City realtor Barbara from New Jersey. She was trying to figure out a way to distinguish herself from the masses. She came up with an idea which was to take her own sales data, the only window she has into the Manhattan real estate market at that time is what she is what her clients are buying and selling, which she's facilitating. She has that data, is going up or down relative to last year. She puts all this data together in what she calls the Corcoran Report, and she starts sending the Corcoran Report out to the New York Times and the New York Post and whatever. (01:25:18): Because nobody else at the time was putting together a report on the health of the Manhattan real estate market, everyone started reporting on the Corcoran Report as if it was an authoritative thing. It's produced by Barbara Corcoran, which immediately put her in the position of being an authority in this space. That was so smart, and I see it happen all the time. (01:25:37): My inbox will also be filled with, for example, a company that specializes in remote work consulting. Especially remote work consulting, you can hire them, it's a B2B service. It's hard to get press for that, here's what they do. They pay a surveying firm to find all sorts of things. The top states for remote work, the top companies for remote work, the top whatever for remote work. They produce all these surveys and they send the surveys out. The surveys get covered because now they're creating a piece of news. They're creating some context in which they just happen to live in. Hard to write about them, this random company, but you write about the survey, that's interesting stuff. Oh, it turns out that Utah is the top, I don't know if that's true, is the top state for, that's something that people will write about. You're giving people things to write about. Then once they do that, you are a part of the story. I get those pitches all the time. I occasionally bite on them and Fred from Ripple Rug got himself a big feature as a result.
turns.zh: 她通过创立一家名为Corcoran的房地产公司——为买卖双方提供服务——积累了财富。她建立这家公司的方式非常有趣。芭芭拉，在成为Corcoran房地产公司的芭芭拉·科科兰之前，她只是新泽西州的一名普通纽约市房地产经纪人。她试图在众多同行中脱颖而出。她想到了一个主意：利用自己掌握的销售数据（当时她获取曼哈顿房地产市场动态的唯一窗口）——客户买卖的房产信息——来制作一份报告。她将这些数据与去年同期对比，整理成《Corcoran报告》，并将其发送给《纽约时报》和《纽约邮报》等媒体。（01:25:18）由于当时没有其他人系统性地分析曼哈顿房地产市场健康状况，媒体纷纷引用《Corcoran报告》，视其为权威数据。这让芭芭拉·科科兰迅速成为该领域的权威专家。这种策略真是高明，我见证过无数类似案例。（01:25:37）我的收件箱里也常收到类似推送，比如某家专注远程工作咨询的公司。特别是远程工作咨询服务，属于B2B业务。这种业务很难获得媒体报道，但他们另辟蹊径：委托调查公司收集各类数据——远程工作最热门的州、最受欢迎的公司等——并将调查结果发布出去。这些数据因具有新闻价值而受到关注，为品牌创造了曝光契机。人们会报道“犹他州成为远程工作最热门州”之类的独家新闻。这种策略能激发人们的创作热情。一旦媒体报道了这些数据，公司便能顺势成为新闻焦点。我常收到这类推销邮件，Ripple Rug公司就曾因此获得了大型专题报道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing other strategy. I imagine if I was a founder, I'd be like, "Hmm, what trends can I think about that I can tap into?"
turns.zh: 这真是个绝妙的策略。我想如果我是创业者，我可能会想：“嗯，我能挖掘哪些值得利用的趋势呢？”

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah. Sometimes you have it in your own data. If you have a lot of data, you might, Zapier. Zapier is a great example. I get a pitch from Zapier every single year about the fastest growing business apps of the year based on Zapier data because they see what people are using and they just compile that together into a top 10 list and people run it. It's very smart.
turns.zh: 是啊。有时你能在自己的数据中发现机会。比如Zapier公司。他们每年都会根据平台数据发布年度增长最快的商业应用榜单，吸引了大量关注。这种策略非常聪明。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. We've gone through all three steps. Is there anything else that you wanted to touch on that we haven't touched on? Anything else that you think would be really valuable for founders or product leaders trying to get press that we haven't already shared?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我们已经完成了这三个步骤。还有没有其他你想补充的，我们之前没有提到的？有没有你认为对那些试图获得媒体报道的创始人或产品负责人非常有价值的内容，我们还没有分享过？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: This has come up in different ways, but I'll just put a point on it as a maybe final way of thinking about this. Be human, be human. Press releases don't work because they're not human. I don't like interviewing people who are on talking points because that's not human. You're ultimately engaging in a human business. A subjective decision is being made about how to serve an audience of humans. There's no right or wrong. There's no way to know. Media is a sort of barely data-driven industry because every story is kind of different. It's like it's hard. It's hard to optimize the product because the product changes every minute. You're dealing with humans and the more that you can be human in every step of this process, when you pitch, write a human email, don't write a thing that looks like it came off of some marketing copy. Write a human email to another human and then when that person engages with you, be very human with them. (01:28:26): I mean, Lenny, the reason why that fast company reporter liked you, I am very sure was because when they got on the phone with you, you were just like a normal nice guy. If you presented yourself differently because you just wanted to frame yourself in some way or you felt protective or something or whatever it was, the reporter would've thought, "This guy is a dick," and he would've written a totally different story.
turns.zh: 这个问题以不同的方式被提过，但我还是想再强调一点，可能是最后的思考方向。保持人性化，保持人性化。新闻稿之所以没用，就是因为不够人性化。我不喜欢采访那些只会照本宣科的人，那样太不人性化了。你最终是在经营一个人类业务。如何服务受众是主观决定的，没有对错之分，也无法预知结果。媒体行业在某种程度上是数据驱动型的，但每个故事又各不相同。这很难优化产品，因为产品每分钟都在变化。你面对的是人类，在这个过程的每一步都要尽可能保持人性化——推销产品时，写邮件时，不要写得像营销文案，要像人对人地交流。（01:28:26）：比如，《快公司》的记者之所以喜欢你，我很确定是因为当他们和你通电话时，你就是个普通的好人。如果你表现得不同——比如为了塑造某种形象，或者显得防备心太强之类的——记者会觉得“这家伙真讨厌”，然后写出完全不同的报道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Be as human as you can and you will be dealing with a human who will receive that.
turns.zh: 尽可能保持人性化，这样对方也会感受到你的真诚。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing advice. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round.
turns.zh: 太棒的建议了。到此为止，我们要进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you ready?
turns.zh: 准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 开始吧。你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. What are two or three books that you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 安德鲁·陈的《冷启动难题》，我反复向别人推荐这本书，因为里面关于网络效应的教训非常棒。最近我和很多创业者聊焦虑和完美主义的问题，一本叫《完美主义者的失控指南》的书，作者是心理治疗师凯瑟琳·摩根·沙夫勒，我觉得这本书读起来很棒。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Andrew Chen's, The Cold Start Problem has come up over and over again for me because they're just really great lessons about network effects. I've been having a lot of conversations about anxiety and perfectionism with entrepreneurs lately, and a book by a psychotherapist named Katherine Morgan Schafler called The Perfectionist's Guide to Losing Control, is, I think, just a really great read.
turns.zh: 太酷了。最近你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Super cool. What is a favorite recent movie or TV show that you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 电影？我最近很少看电影。我有两个小孩，但我带八岁的孩子去看了新版《忍者神龟》，很棒，能重温童年喜欢的角色真是太棒了。然后我和妻子终于看完了《风骚律师》，虽然晚了好多年，但真是完美之作。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Movie? I don't get to see a lot of movies these days. I have two little kids, but I took my eight-year old to see the new Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, which was great and a really nice way of, I loved them as a kid, and so it was cool to see the modern version. Then my wife and I just finished Better Call Saul like years late, but it was just perfect.
turns.zh: 我还没看过那部剧呢。我超爱《绝命毒师》。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I haven't watched that series yet. I loved Breaking Bad.
turns.zh: 哦，太值了。你一定要看。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Oh, it's worth it. You got to.
turns.zh: 好的，我得开始看了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Another series I got to get started on.
turns.zh: 好的，我得开始看另一部剧了。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: I know it's too much, too much television.
turns.zh: 我知道这有点过分，看太多电视了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I usually ask this next question too, like product leaders and growth people, but I'm curious what the answer for you would be is. Do you have a favorite interview question you like to ask people you're interviewing? Usually it's about people you're hiring.
turns.zh: 我通常也会问下一个问题——比如产品负责人和增长团队的人——但我很好奇你会给面试者提什么样的问题。你有没有特别喜欢问面试者的某个问题？通常都是关于你要招聘的人的。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Interviewing a job candidate?
turns.zh: 面试求职者？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that's the ideal, but take it either way.
turns.zh: 是啊，这才是理想状态，但无论如何都能接受。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: I'll take it a little bit different because we've been talking about press. This is a really great strategy for interviewing people, and I'm going to tell it to you because I think that it's also good in any other context, and it might be a thing that somebody will do to you in an interview. My favorite strategy for interviewing people is to throw a theory at them, and I don't mean a theory of the world. I mean that maybe 10 minutes in after they have told me a couple different things and answer some different questions, I'll make a connection in my head and I'll say, "I want to run a theory by you. Do you think that the reason why you are really interested in this or you made that decision is actually because of this other thing that you told me a little bit about?" (01:30:59): You're listening. It's really active listening, and you're combining things together into some theory. The reason why the theory works so well is because it forces people to think in real time in front of you. I like that because I often interview people who have been interviewed a million times before. I interview Jimmy Fallon and The Rock and whatever. They've been interviewed a million times before, so how do you get them to think in front of you? The answer is to ask them the thing that they haven't been asked. What I love about the theory is that it shows them that you're really listening and you're trying to understand them. "It's so interesting that you did that. I wonder if it's because of," X, Y, Z thing. That gets them to react in a really earnest honest way. (01:31:49): I would say for what it's worth, as a job candidate tactic, it's not that bad either. My favorite job interview that I ever did as a candidate that I didn't even get the job was years and years ago, I interviewed for a job at New York Magazine. I interviewed with Adam Moss, who is not there anymore, but he was the legendary editor in chief. He made me, on the spot, drill down specifically into an idea. He was like, "What's your favorite section in Strategists," which is one of the sections of magazine. I was like, "I really like the real estate section." He's like, "All right, what would be a good neighborhood that we should feature in the real estate section?" I was like, "Oh, I don't know," I named a neighborhood. He's like, "What would be three good elements of that?" He just kept pushing me, drill down, drill down, drill down. There was no right or wrong answer. He just wanted to see how I thought. I found that to be incredibly powerful, and I do a version of that when I interview people.
turns.zh: 我会稍微换个角度，因为我们一直在谈论新闻采访。这确实是面试人的一个很棒的策略，我要告诉你，因为我觉得它在任何其他情境下也很有用，而且可能有人会在面试中用这招对我。面试人的最佳策略就是向他们抛出一个理论，我不是指世界观理论。我是说，在他们讲了几分钟不同的事情、回答了几个不同问题之后，我会在脑子里建立联系，然后说：“我想和你探讨一个理论。你觉得你对这个如此感兴趣或者做出那个决定的原因，实际上是因为你之前告诉我的一些其他事情吗？”（01:30:59）：你在听。这是真正的积极倾听，你把各种信息整合成某种理论。这种理论之所以效果如此之好，因为它迫使人们在你面前实时思考。我喜欢这样，因为我经常面试那些被面试过无数次的人。我采访过吉米·法伦、巨石强森之类的。他们被面试过无数次，所以如何让他们在你面前思考？答案就是问他们没被问过的问题。我喜欢这个理论的地方在于，它向他们表明你真的在倾听，真的在试图理解他们。“你这么做真是太有趣了。我想知道是不是因为……”X、Y、Z。这会让他们以一种非常真诚、诚实的方式做出反应。（01:31:49）：我要说，就算不算什么，拿来当求职者的策略也不错。我最喜欢的一次求职面试是多年前的，我甚至没得到那份工作。我面试了《纽约杂志》的工作。我面试的对象是亚当·莫斯，他现在不在那里了，但他曾是传奇主编。他当场让我深入探讨一个想法。他问：“《战略家》杂志里你最喜欢的板块是什么？” 这是杂志的板块之一。我说：“我真的很喜欢房地产板块。” 他说：“好，那房地产板块应该重点介绍哪个社区？” 我说：“哦，我不知道。” 我说了一个社区。他说：“那社区的三个亮点是什么？” 他就一直追问我，深入探讨，深入探讨，深入探讨。没有正确或错误的答案。他只是想看看我的思考过程。我觉得这非常有效，我面试别人时也会用这种方法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I love that. What is a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我喜欢这个。你最近发现的自己特别喜欢的某个产品是什么？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: I use BIGVU, I don't even know how to pronounce it, BIGVU, B-I-G-V-U, all the time. It's a teleprompter app. I spent like $150 buying an actual teleprompter because I make a lot of video and that teleprompter is, it's actually for people who are just listening to this, I'm pointing at another desk across my room where it's sitting there and I've never used it. The reason is because then I discovered BIGVU, which is just a app that runs a teleprompter very close to the camera, either in horizontal or vertical mode. I've tested it out in a million different ways, and it really works like you're reading it and it really looks like you're looking directly at the camera. I love it. It has saved me so much time.
turns.zh: 我用BIGVU这款应用，我甚至都不知道怎么读它的名字，BIGVU，B-I-G-V-U，一直在用。这是一款提词器应用。我花了150美元买了一个真正的提词器，因为我经常拍视频，但那个提词器实际上是给那些只听我讲话的人准备的，我指着房间另一边的桌子，那个提词器就放在那里，但我从没用过它。原因是我后来发现了BIGVU这款应用，它能让提词器紧贴镜头运行，横屏或竖屏模式都可以。我用了无数种方法测试过，它效果真的很棒——就像你亲自在读台词一样，看着镜头的感觉特别自然。我超爱它，它帮我节省了大量时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is cool. You basically put your phone on your screen next to the camera or wherever your camera is?
turns.zh: 太酷了。你基本上是把手机放在屏幕上，紧贴镜头或者摄像头所在的位置？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: No, no, no. This would be for if you're recording, if you're recording on the phone.
turns.zh: 不不不。这是针对拍摄视频时用的，比如用手机拍摄的时候。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. You're staring at the phone and it's telling you what to say. I get it.
turns.zh: 明白了。你盯着手机，它会提示你该说什么。我懂了。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: You write a script and then you just import the script and then you choose the speed and you can fuss with it, how many words per minute, and then it'll run the text very close to where the camera lens is.
turns.zh: 你写好剧本后，就可以导入，然后调整语速，还能调整每分钟的字数，这样文字就会显示在镜头附近。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. All right.
turns.zh: 太神奇了。好吧。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to check that out. What is a favorite life motto that you'd like to repeat yourself, share with friends, something that comes up a lot,
turns.zh: 我想问你一个最喜欢的的人生格言，供你自己反思，也能分享给朋友，经常挂在嘴边的那种。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Something that I've been repeating a lot to people is something that I heard, so I recommended Katherine's book, The Perfectionist Guide to Losing Control. I met Katherine because I, we've since become friends, but I interviewed her for the podcast when her book came out. We were talking about feeling overworked and being stretched too thin, and she gave me this question, which I think about almost daily, and I repeat to people all the time, and that is, "What's the point of building something if you can't maintain it?" I love that question because I, like probably everyone listening to this, pushes themselves really hard, and at some point you have to step back and think, "Am I building something where at some point there is sustainability for me here, or is this unsustainable and what's the point of building something if you can't maintain it?" It's a great reminder for why you're building something and how you have to build it.
turns.zh: 我经常跟别人说的一句话是从凯瑟琳的书《完美主义者指南：学会放手》中听到的。我认识凯瑟琳是因为采访她，她的书出版后，我采访了她。我们聊到工作过度、精力透支的问题，她给了我一个问题，我现在几乎每天都在想，也经常跟别人分享：“如果你建造的东西无法维持，那还有什么意义？”我很喜欢这个问题，因为我和听众可能一样，拼命往前冲，但有时必须退后想：“我建造的东西，能让我在这里可持续发展吗？还是说它不可持续？如果无法维持，那还有什么意义？”这很好地提醒了你为什么要建造，以及如何建造。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I have a very similar quote that my sister's partner once said that has stuck with me forever, which is, "Life is maintenance. Basically everything that you buy or bring into your life, you have to maintain."
turns.zh: 我有个很相似的引语，是我姐姐的伴侣说的，让我刻骨铭心：“生活就是维护。基本上你买进来或带入生活的任何东西，都需要维护。”

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We got a new air conditioner. Now, we have a guy that comes every year to check it. You got a generator, someone's got to check that thing all the time. We got a toy, now I got to think about where does it go and do we throw it away? Do we keep it? Everything that you bring into your life, you have to maintain basically for the rest.
turns.zh: 我们新买了空调。现在每年都有人来检查。买了发电机后，就得一直有人维护。买了玩具后，又得考虑放在哪儿，扔掉还是留着？你带进生活的任何东西，都需要维护。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah, it's really true.
turns.zh: 是啊，这确实是真的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, so it's really, I think specifically for work, it's like you start a new project, you're going to have to-
turns.zh: 是啊，所以我觉得特别是对于工作而言，当你启动一个新项目时，就必须——

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: You're going to have to maintain it.
turns.zh: 你得去维护它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... maintain it, like this podcast, right? It's like, do you want to start a podcast and do it forever?
turns.zh: ……去维护它，比如这个播客，对吧？你会不会想开个播客，然后永远做下去？

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a part of it. Part starting something is you have to maintain it.
turns.zh: 这就是其中一部分。开始做某件事的一部分，就是你必须去维护它。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Jason Feifer
turns.en: I know we're in the lightning round and we've defied the logic of lightning rounds, but I'll just add one other thing to that, which is that I interviewed Michelle Pfeiffer for the cover of the magazine, and one of the things that I thought was most fascinating was that she started this fragrance company, and it's called Henry Rose. She said the major difference between making movies and building a company that she found, was that when you make a movie, all the work happens in the beginning. You make the movie and then the movie is out, and then you are done. You don't have to work on the movie ever again. She was not really mentally prepared for a company being the exact opposite, that the launch of the company is actually the start of the work and there's an endlessness to it. She said that it took her a solid year to adapt to that reality, and then it became fun. I think it's the thing people forget.
turns.zh: 我知道我们现在是在闪电问答环节，而且我们违背了闪电问答的逻辑，但我还是想再补充一点。我为杂志封面采访了米歇尔·菲佛，我觉得最有趣的一点是，她创办了一家香水公司，叫Henry Rose。她说，她发现拍电影和创办公司最大的区别在于，拍电影时，所有工作都在前期完成。拍完电影，电影上映了，然后就结束了。你不需要再为电影做任何工作。但创办公司恰恰相反，公司的启动才是真正工作的开始，而且永无止境。她说她花了整整一年时间才适应这种现实，然后才发现这其实很有趣。我觉得这就是人们容易忽视的一点。

It could be starting a podcast because you like listening to podcasts, anything. What am I doing now that is leading me to something else? I'm the only one who can figure it out.

（01:38:58）：我接手《创业者》杂志时，编辑部零人，没人对我说：“你应该去演讲巡回。应该擅长播客采访。应该写本书。”没人这么说。我的工作是做出一本好杂志，指导品牌编辑方向，但所有这些机会都摆在我面前。一旦意识到这一点，我发现自己可以去追寻它们，这样做也能重新审视自我。我还是杂志编辑吗？不再是了。这只是我现在做的一件事。我认为自己是个创业者，一个致力于帮助他人的创业者。这就是我对自己的定位。我能走到今天，只因为我思考着：我现在在这里，所以我能到达那里。没人会要求我去做。我必须自己行动。这是我一直思考的问题，也是让我夜不能寐的问题：我现在做的事情能带我走向何方？只有我自己能找出答案。
